Its first article makes the Secretary of Defense the Executive Agent for the program, acting under policies agreed jointly with the Director. The aim stated is full use of the talents and resources found in both the Defense Department and the Agency.

To carry that charge, the Secretary sets up the National Reconnaissance Office as a separate operating agency of the Defense Department, under his direction and control. Its Director comes from the Defense side, named with the Director of Central Intelligence concurring, and gives most of his time to the Office. Its Deputy Director comes from CIA, named the same way in reverse, keeping the balance between the two houses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400070001-8:
Copy of the defence and CIA agreement on management of the National Reconnaissance Program survives in a scan rougher than most. It gives the Deputy Director of the NRO a defined place in the chain of command. He sits directly under the Director and must be kept fully and currently informed on all program activity at all times. Under the Director's hand he supervises ties with the United States Intelligence Board and its committees.

He also supervises all program tasks the Director assigns to CIA, and acts with the Director's full powers during absence or disability. Staff from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and CIA fill NRO posts full time. The chain of command runs from the Secretary of Defense, as Executive Agent, straight to the Director, and a functions section opens with work on a single national program of collection projects.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400130004-8:
Memorandum for the record dated 25 August 1961 sets down basic understandings between CIA and the Department of the Air Force on procurement under Project OXCART and KEDLOCK contracts. It builds on January 1956 letters between Trevor Gardner and Allen Dulles, a February 1956 record on AQUATONE buying, and the February 1960 OXCART organisation agreement signed by Dulles and General White.

The understandings renew a proven channel: CIA's special contract methods buy supplies and services the Air Force needs, in ways both sides found gainful under AQUATONE. CIA negotiates each contract from written Air Force requirements, and the Air Force side confirms each deal fits those requirements in full. Policy and procedure on such contracts follow the practice already in force on CIA's own OXCART procurements of the same kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400320003-8:
Memorandum dated 1 April 1967, sent to the Director of the National Reconnaissance Office, adds the case for moving the IDEALIST project to Davis Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona. It supplements a study of 14 March 1967 that listed reasons the move was not feasible. The memo instead lists advantages that might follow, on the same assumptions and with building costs at the new base accepted.

Chief gain named is closure of North Base at Edwards Air Force Base, possible once U-2R testing is largely done in about two years. The writer is candid that savings would be small: runway upkeep and fire protection are the main items, and support costs would rise at Davis Monthan as they fell at Edwards. Shared maintenance for the two U-2 fleets is raised, though sensor control must stay separate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400350028-8:
Memorandum for the record dated 13 April 1958 reports a personal equipment staff visit to Edwards and Del Rio Air Force Bases. Pilot morale is found good, and trust in the personal equipment staff acceptable. One sore point stood out: pilots assumed the project had let their gear slide, and that SAC pilots at Del Rio held far better kit.

A check at Del Rio showed the gear there was not superior, and the sore points were talked through with the pilots. Facility work to rebuild the pre-breathing, maintenance, and storage areas began on 31 March 1958. A long section covers ejection seats: all project aircraft are to get hot seats, at a weight penalty of fifty-three pounds, with hot and cold seats kept interchangeable in each aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400350118-8:
Letter dated 1 September 1955, on Air Force Office of Scientific Research letterhead from Baltimore, writes to the project's Deputy Director about aeromedical support. The writer sums up points settled in informal talks over the past month, and offers his reading of the agreements for correction if any item seems off. Medical responsibility is the first item taken up.

A project surgeon is to be assigned to the unit, working solely for it, with policy guidance flowing only through the Surgeon General, Major General Dan Ogle. The writer will brief the surgeon on past aeromedical work and on staffing needs. He presses hard on delays in getting medical airmen requested months before, fearing a crisis at first screening. A meeting on the scope of the professional support contract linked to Dr Lovelace is also being arranged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500060001-8:
Memorandum for General Ross forwards comments on U-2R carrier operations drawn from watching BLUE GULL V aboard USS America in November 1969. The verdict is favourable: the operation was well executed. The first landings were made in weather short of the best. The writer takes that as proof that flying the aircraft from a carrier deck is feasible. No problem arose that the crew could not handle.

Safety notes follow. Pilots should be trained to close the speed brakes on arrestment, since deck hands working near the hook stand inside their arc. The Navy norm of two landing signal officers, not the one used here, is urged for training and for spotting bad trends early. A pre-deployment briefing by ship's company, squeezed out this time, should be restored, and a named contact should man the ready room.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390104-8:
Memorandum GUS-0110, dated 29 January 1959, passes reconnaissance design guidelines for GUSTO to the Deputy Director for Plans. Two starting points shape the guidance: approval for long range penetration flights will stay hard to obtain, and each such flight must bring back the most information possible.

Only passive equipment should be used, the memo argues, ruling out radar sets that could reveal the aircraft. Two design paths follow, mixing visual photography with other sensors, or relying on sensors alone for poor weather and night work. Camera options for clear and adverse conditions are compared. The memo closes by urging early talks between camera designers and vehicle builders.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040039-8:
Weekend and holiday cover at Detachment H is defined in SOP H-20-3, dated 21 June 1968. The Staff Duty Officer is the point for choices and actions on off-duty days. He keeps the unit able to react while most staff are away. The Director of Support puts out the duty roster well ahead of time, where that can be done.

Duty officers may swap tours if Support hears of the change by noon on the last work day. The officer on duty must stay on base and tell section heads where he can be found. Choices on policy or flying go up to the commander or the operations chief first. A log form for each tour is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070018-8:
Keeping test project records, and clearing them out at the end, is governed by standing operating procedure 50-3055-20, dated 14 December 1964. Records means all papers created or picked up in support of a named test project. Each project has its own file, run by a Project Test Director, with a records officer watching the system as a whole for the organization.

Three rules open the policy: project papers must be complete, significant facts must be findable at any time, and files must be kept in a set order. Folder sections cover authority and program papers, test plans and procedures, travel support, test data, upkeep data, and system faults. Cover formats and contents lists are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050037-8:
Development Projects Division directive 10-2, dated 5 June 1962, tightens access to the DPD controlled area in the headquarters building. A letter K on a building badge had allowed free entry at all hours, and requests for it were rising fast. Action was taken to cut the number of non-DPD staff holding that free access to the 6B Wing restricted area.

Three groups are set instead. K is kept for DPD staff and others with a clear need for free entry. A second group goes on an access list and receives a temporary non-escort badge from the receptionist, with visits logged. Others enter as occasional visitors. Later papers cover contractor visits and care with classified material left out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020002-8:
Quarterly progress packet sent 16 January 1969 by Donald H. Ross covers OXCART and IDEALIST from 1 October to 31 December 1968. Tab A is a phase-out summary: OXCART property records were handled during a December period named in the text, as the closed program's affairs were settled. The packet carries five copies of each report for the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs.

IDEALIST work includes an engine pressure ratio schedule drawn from Pratt and Whitney study of flight test data. The schedule in use was judged too cautious, and a new one was being built from Detachment G data, to be checked at Detachment H for stall-free running in cold air. Film and filter tests for the wider intelligence community are also reported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800030001-8:
Memorandum 9258-72, dated 13 October 1972, forwards the IDEALIST progress report for 1 July to 30 September 1972. Wendell L. Bevan Jr. signs as Director of Special Activities. Three copies go to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. The report's development section leads with flight testing and qualification work under way during the summer quarter.

One delay is spelled out. The first modified B-3 camera with a new lens will arrive late in the second quarter. Its lens aspheric surface needs rework to fix a misalignment of its axis. Life support items include a new survival weapon folded into the seat kit, taking far less space than the old one. The semiannual life support conference, held in Washington on 2 August 1972, is also reported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800100003-8:
Status slides for IDEALIST, covering 1 April to 30 June 1971, list test flying at Detachment G, Edwards Air Force Base. Red Dot film tests used varied camera fits in the U-2C and U-2R, over eleven sorties. Other work included one hurricane photography sortie over Gulf Coast areas for the Office of Emergency Preparedness. Three sorties qualified a light weight monitor system. Two thermal tests of the Q bay were also flown.

A second slide set covers Detachment H for the same quarter. It reports fourteen missions alerted and eight flown. A note states that flown missions stayed at least twenty nautical miles off the coast of China. That limit matched an overflight suspension set by the 40 Committee, as the slide records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250007-8:
Memorandum 8914-68, dated 5 July 1968, gives the OXCART operational summary for 1 April to 30 June 1968. One A-12 overflight was flown in the period, launching from and returning to Kadena Air Base, Okinawa. The mission made two passes over targets in North Korea, with a flight time of 4 hours 6 minutes, as printed in the summary.

Fifteen SAM sites were covered: three occupied, one unoccupied, and eleven for identification only. Photo quality over the southern two-fifths of North Korea was fair to poor, with haze and cloud over about half the take. The summary notes this was the final BLACK SHIELD operational mission. Later pages cover redeployment from Kadena and nine A-12 aircraft placed in storage at Palmdale.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250016-8:
Progress packet 2691-67, signed by Paul N. Bacalis, forwards OXCART and IDEALIST reports for 1 July to 30 September 1967. Five copies of each go to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. Status tables place A-12 aircraft and pilots at Kadena Air Base, Okinawa, and note that aircraft 122 entered flyable storage at Palmdale on 16 September 1967, as the attachment records.

The IDEALIST section marks a milestone: the first flight of the U-2R took place at Edwards Air Force Base, California, on 25 August 1967, with more flights since. A visit to Pratt and Whitney follows in the propulsion section. Closing research notes cover a proposal to cut induced drag on high altitude aircraft, forwarded to the Director, National Reconnaissance Office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100090006-8:
Administrative Service, Office of the Chief, presents a statement of functions with a table of organization and position status headings. The chief's office holds overall coordination, supervision, policy, procedures, and general management of the service's divisions. It also runs liaison with CIA activities and other bodies named in the text, as the statement records.

Because the service's work is spread across many buildings, the chief and his two deputies follow a visiting schedule. Each of them visits two divisions per week, to talk through current and coming programs and problems. The file repeats the statement and contents pages across several scanned pages, with the same headings carried through each copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030119-8:
CIA procedure regulation on building maintenance and utilities, departmental area, tells offices how to ask for alterations and installations in agency buildings. Requests go to the Chief, Administrative Services, on Form No. 36-7 or by memorandum in duplicate. They should state the service needed and its justification in specific terms, with drawings or sketches where practical, and name a contact person for the work.

The Building Maintenance and Utilities Division supplies engineers when needed and helps plan projects. Work touching the physical security of an area is sent for recommendation or approval before action. Further sections cover real estate and construction beyond the departmental area, with requests routed to the Real Estate and Construction Division. A reproduction section at the end repeats the rule that signed requests go to the Reproduction Division chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030128-8:
CIA regulation on reproduction requires each office head to name staff, at GS-7 or above, who may authorize reproduction services for that office. Names go in writing to the Chief, Administrative Services, and changes must also be reported in writing. The point is control of demand on the agency's reproduction plant, which the regulation calls heavy.

Authorized staff must learn the services on offer, the time each takes, and its cost, so the cheapest suitable process is chosen and copy counts kept low. All signed requests go to the chief of the Reproduction Division. Equipment requests route through that chief as well. Later sections in the file cover telephone and teletype requests, cafeteria liaison, and hot plate installation, which requires a fireproof base and a checked power circuit before use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050036-8:
Federal Register issue for Friday, 22 December 1950, volume 15, number 248, is bound into this file as printed pages. Its lead item under Title 3, The President, is Executive Order 10195. That order names Korea and adjacent waters a combat zone for income tax purposes. It acts under section 22(b)(13) of the Internal Revenue Code, as amended by the Revenue Act of 1950.

The zone is drawn by coordinates. It runs from latitude 39 degrees 30 minutes north down the 122 degrees 45 minutes east line. It then crosses to 133 degrees east, and up to the coast where Korea meets the USSR. Later pages carry other register matter. Transportation allowance rules set net weight at eighty percent of packed weight. Agriculture conservation payment rates for pipe by diameter also appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050144-8:
Memorandum for the Chief, Services Branch, marked as reviewed by the Office of General Counsel on 25 November 1947, returns a redraft of proposed delegations of authority with suggested changes underlined. Wording points lead: the title Director of Central Intelligence is restored, matching the original delegation, and one word is swapped because the first suggested text above it in the same paper. A specific rescission clause is added, and renumbering is proposed.

The delegation text follows. Its root is a Director's memorandum of 24 July 1947. The Chief or Assistant Chief, Supply Division, may sign unnumbered contracts where payment is a single remittance under 2,000 dollars. The draft stresses that no exception to the single payment rule exists for this agency, so contracting officers, contractors, and the General Accounting Office are all on notice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050171-8:
Agreement dated 27 November 1946 moves the State Department printing plant at 2430 E Street, Northwest, to the Government Printing Office. The three parties are the Department of State, the Central Intelligence Group, and the Government Printing Office. The plant is transferred and will be operated by the printing office under 44 U.S.C. 60, subject to the agreement's terms.

A list of plant staff and equipment to move will go to a policy committee for concurrence. Extra equipment and staff needed for sound running will be supplied by the printing office. In running the plant, the printing office will follow the security rules of State or the Central Intelligence Group, whichever is higher for the work in hand. Payment for work is under section 601 of the Economy Act. The transfer takes effect on or before 1 March 1947.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050199-8:
Annotated edition of the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, issued by the General Services Administration under Administrator Jess Larson, pairs the act's text with analysis and a full index. The act's contents run from organization of the new administration through property management: buying and warehousing, use of excess property, surplus disposal, proceeds, and surveys, standardization, and cataloging.

The analysis explains section by section why provisions read as they do. One note on uncollectible claims stresses the wide discretion staff need when vast amounts of property must be moved swiftly. Civil penalties for fraud are analyzed, with three measures of damages open to the United States. The index closes the volume, running from personnel holding appointments under the Surplus Property Act of 1944 to warehousing and woolen goods disposal, with section numbers for each entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200070043-8:
Draft procedures dated January 1949, written under a memorandum of 29 December 1948 from the Executive Director, govern handling of signal property by the Services Office and the Communications Division, OSO. Accountability records will be kept in the Storage and Issue Section of the Supply Division. The Communications Division will keep its own memorandum record of stock on hand, posted from requisitions. Copies of all vouchers posted by the accountable officer will be sent to it for information.

Nomenclature comes next. The two offices will review all signal equipment on hand and fix complete, accurate names for every item, with a stock numbering system agreed between them. Receiving is a Services Office duty; technical inspection belongs to the Inspection and Testing Section. Shipments are coordinated with the Transportation Section, and cancellations must be reported by memorandum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100003-8:
Monthly report of operations for the period ending 31 August 1953, from the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch. Personnel figures show eighteen Mail Control staff on leave of three days or more, ten in Records Management, and three at the Records Center. One man is detailed full time as a courier to the Transportation Division. New applicants interviewed and recruiting by office and by Personnel are also tabled.

Administration notes lead with meetings with two groups of area records officers. Points at issue between the branch and the offices are mostly settled, the report states, and the assignment should finish within the next month. Project 5-53, rewriting the CIA Correspondence Manual, has been revised after agency comments and will circulate through area records officers. Filming for the month totals 23,978 images: 3,780 by rotary camera and 20,198 by flatbed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100020027-8:
Office memorandum dated 25 January 1949, headed random notes on the TRS reorganization, argues staffing points for the Office of Deputy for Special Projects. An administrative officer is needed on that staff at least half time. One named staff member now spends about seventy-five percent of her time on such problems, the notes say. She has become the person everyone turns to when anything needs doing, and an unmatched source on training problems across Buildings 13 and 14.

A clerk-stenographer is called urgent, in line with a memo of 12 January 1949. Tests and measurements staffing is also pressed: an instructor with a degree in educational psychology, strong on test construction, is wanted. The writer notes he gives two to four hours a day to OPC interests, with no OPC officer provided on the staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020041-8:
Results of a conference of 22 July 1952 record agreements between the head of IT/D and the Plans and Policy Staff. The subject is the Career Service Committee report's effect on the Basic Intelligence Course. The conference worked from P&P notes. All statements of the situation in them were accepted. On the program's objective, doubt should clear once a definition of professional enters a CIA regulation. The 14 July draft was accepted.

On specialized skills, TR(G) will wait and see. The head of IT/D leans more on on-the-job training than P&P. Student numbers beyond the capacity of Alcott Wing B are to be planned for. Staff totals are nine CIA staff, four from other agencies, and a training assistant. Space ratios close the paper: one classroom for each twenty-five to thirty students, and no more than two instructors to an office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100040004-8:
National Security Council directive, issued under section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947 as amended, sets the rules that govern United States work in this field. Council changes and additions, based on Agency advice the statute calls for, are provided for in the opening text. The Agency's reach covers all government work of this kind tied to national security, the directive states. It also states plainly what the Agency lacks: no police, subpoena, or law work, and no internal security role.

Production duties follow. The Agency turns out work inside its own charge, plus work not otherwise to be had that its tasks and other agencies' tasks require. Before general release, it will normally ask the department concerned to read its reports and estimates for that department's views. Fast action on Agency deadlines is called a must, with first priority given to the Director's requests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100060039-8:
Program for a visit of Army and Air attaches designate to the Foreign Service Institute's School of Diplomatic and Consular Practices, dated 25 February, runs a full study day. A motion picture on operation of an overseas mission opens at the school's G Street rooms. Talks follow: coordination at the foreign service post, economic aspects of foreign policy by the Institute's director, and problems of foreign policy from the Policy Reports Staff. An afternoon session covers coordination of intelligence activities, then conferences with geographic desk officers and with intelligence and research officers.

A roster of the attaches designate is bound with the program, naming colonels, majors, and captains with their services. Biographic information was set for an afternoon appointment, the routing note states. Follow on pages list further meetings by room and hour, with named State Department officers for China affairs, geographic information, and Far East research among the contacts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140012-8:
Tabular companion to the January 1952 survey lists outside training office by office in short entries. O/RR shows its ten hour opening lecture, monthly for twenty students with eleven instructors, and its film training for analysts. O/SI reports on-the-job training for all new staff. An internal opening course is in preparation, for newcomers with at least three weeks in the office. The Foreign Documents Division offers a first Russian course of three months, one hour each morning on set days, to give clerical staff a basic Russian facility.

Radio and cipher entries repeat the course data: staff radio training, secret radio, and a secret cipher course of no fixed length, taught as instructors allow. Closing pages turn to O/CI items, some planned for 1952. They name source work, trips to exploit sensitive sources, area background study for analysts, and an exchange with the Foreign Service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000100040078-8:
Weekly Activity Report dated 16 July 1953 gives progress on old projects of the training staff. An instructor training course has been approved by the DD/TR(S). It will run in three phases: a course of study, on-the-job training, and lasting watch over the new instructors' methods. Details are in hand, with a target date of 15 September. A mobile audio-visual aids device was shown to staff; their comments will feed the design of a second prototype, to be built by TSS.

The OSS film footage project has sorted negative and positive material from the Library of Congress collection. Early scanning shows little of value, the report states. A basic agent tradecraft manual is in translation at FDD, seven chapters in hand. A glossary called The Red Interpreter has gone forward with a cost estimate and a request for funds to print it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200020015-8:
Explanation of a revised training evaluation form sets out the purposes and principles behind the change, and asks for further suggestions. The draft is still tentative; one more revision is planned. It is hoped the next form will last for some time. The form is built to report results from many kinds of courses in one consistent way. That ends constant reprinting as courses change. Where a course needs more, a specific report will supplement the form.

The method of reporting shows what was tested, and the conditions of the test. A line is drawn between what was taught and tested as knowledge or skill, and what was merely observed. Section II rates knowledge, with fields such as principles and methods, and the world situation. Closing rating texts run from a barely adequate performance to an extremely competent one few have surpassed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100020026-8:
Legal Staff memorandum dated 20 October 1950. It went to the Assistant Director, OPC. The subject is death and disability payments. The payments concern alien trainees hurt on duty. Being an alien does not bar a trainee by itself. A trainee in the United States can still claim under the compensation act. Being called a trainee does not end the matter either. Such a person may still count as an Agency employee.

Three classes of trainee are worked through. Some are plainly employees, with full rights. Some are plainly not employees at all. For those, a share might still be paid on policy grounds. A third class works as independent contractors. They get nothing as of right. Later pages quote the Act at length. Rates, medical care, and retraining are all covered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040007-8:
Functions and activities statement, Assessment and Evaluation Staff. Three branches make up the staff. They are the Assessment Branch and Training Evaluation Branch. A Research and Validation Branch completes the set. The staff coordinates all psychological services for training. It runs those services for the Office of Training. Professional help goes to the Director on request.

Programs run inside the United States. Facilities and staffs are organized for that work. Overseas programs get help and supervision. The Professional Selection Panel receives staff help. Other Agency parts may receive help too. Deep study of referred people is one task. Fitness for sensitive posts is the key question. Analysts study success factors in intelligence work. Methods are studied and refined over time. Training records form the other main strand. What a student learned is recorded. Traits shown in training are recorded too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000020006-8:
Letter contract number PC-660 between the Agency and Eastman Kodak. Copy five of six is marked on the file. The form is a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract. Services and supplies are the subject of the order. Exhibit A sets out what must be furnished. The contractor must start work at once on acceptance. Materials must be procured without delay.

Manufacture or performance must proceed with all diligence. Earliest practical delivery is the stated goal. Armed Services Procurement Regulation clauses are built in. They enter by reference, with full force and effect. Definitions and changes clauses are named. Inspection and correction of defects appear too. Assignment of claims and records duties are listed. Exhibit B adds further clauses to the set. Later pages give termination terms in detail. Notice periods and claim deadlines are spelled out. Payment follows the sum found due under those terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080181-8:
Memorandum dated 30 March 1956 from the Agency Project Comptroller. It went to a division chief in the project. Charges on one account were to be moved. The 146.7 account held advances to a contractor. Those charges were to become expenses instead. The 600.1 account was the expense account. Each listed invoice would be charged there. A matching credit would go to the advance account.

Long tables carry the substance of the memo. Invoice numbers fill the first column of each table. Voucher or reference numbers follow the invoices. Dates run through 1955 in the visible tables. Amounts range from about a thousand dollars upward. Several entries pass one hundred thousand dollars. One February entry reads 31,158 dollars exactly. Credits and later invoice runs fill page two. The tables run on for many more entries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000150011-8:
Agency letter contract, copy six, with the contractor unnamed in the head. An order is placed by the opening paragraph. Supplies and services in Exhibit A are covered. The exhibit is made part of the contract. On acceptance, work must proceed at once. Materials must be procured without delay. Manufacture or services must start right away.

Diligence is required until delivery is complete. Earliest practicable delivery is the stated goal. Procurement regulation clauses are built in by reference. Definitions, changes, and extras clauses are named. Variation in quantity and inspection appear too. Responsibility for supplies is covered in the list. Assignment of claims and bond security follow. Tax and disputes clauses are named as well. Termination terms run long in the later text. Failure to agree on a sum is treated. The Contracting Officer can then set the amount. That setting is not the only path allowed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000170118-8:
Memorandum for the record dated 29 June 1956. Amendment number nine to contract A-101 is its subject. The Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation is the contractor. Project AQUATONE is named in the subject line. Air Force work enters the picture in the memo. The Department of the Air Force will join future work. Its funds were not on hand when the memo was written.

Air Force needs were still to reach the project. Approval of a Director of Central Intelligence allotment is sought. That approval covers amendment nine costs. Richard Bissell Jr signed as Project Director. A computations attachment follows the memo text. It tabulates amendment eight and nine figures. Item B-1 rises by 386,830 in the table. Its new total reads as 1,706,976. Item C-1 rises by 103,105 in the table. Item D-1 rises by 200,000 as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000170127-8:
Amendment number nine to Agency contract number A-101. The file is numbered SAPC-7392. The Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation is the contractor named. Work items are changed under the Changes clause. Change order number forty-one lists work to be performed. Estimated cost and fixed fee are both restated. Superseded schedule paragraphs are deleted by the amendment. New paragraphs stand in their place instead.

Research and development items fill the visible changes. One item covers work tied to a CNCC authorization. Additional cost of 10,000 dollars is stated there. Another item amends a sail-related entry. Its estimated cost reads as 10,893 dollars. A system number three item is added as well. Design and development work is its content. Other items adjust earlier amendment eight text. The scan is partly garbled in the figures. Several totals cannot be read with confidence here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100080015-8:
Speech text addressed to an audience of gentlemen. The Office of Training is its subject throughout. The office was nine months old at the time. It had been born in January of that year. Colonel Baird is named as Director of Training. The speaker heads the overt side of the office. A covert side chief is redacted in the text.

The Director directs all Agency training programs. Internal and external programs both fall to him. A career service program is also his charge. High potential staff are recruited under it. Careerists in intelligence are identified and developed. A Special Support Staff handles administrative policy. Language Services forms another office in the account. Intensive eight-week Russian courses are described there. Provisionally cleared staff took those courses. A language laboratory was the office's big hope.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100090041-8:
Address by Professor Anatol James Shneiderov, given 20 March 1952. He was president of the Polycultural Institution of America. The audience sat at the Shoreham Hotel in Washington. Members of the diplomatic corps attended the dinner. Members of Congress attended alongside them. His title is Let Us Be Polycultural. A historical summary forms the body of the talk.

The institution began in a one-room birthplace in 1945. Its childhood was a struggle for existence. The idea came to him in 1944, he relates. He then taught Slavic philology at Johns Hopkins. Russian language teaching filled his class work. Three noted scholars sat among his professor students. Leo Spitzer, Henry Carrington Lancaster, and Kamp Malone are named. A bill seeking twenty-five million dollars is mentioned later. Knowledge of cultures has no practical value alone, he argues. Intercultural cooperation must be understood and desired first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200020001-8:
Agency staff study dated February 1952 for the Training Development Staff. It went to the deputy director for training, covert side. Covert offices need rising operational effectiveness. That need frames the problem of the study. More staff at the same skill level is one path. Higher average skill at the same size is another. Growth in both forms a third path in the study.

Experience alone teaches slowly, the study argues. Losses from attrition eat much of that learning. A better path gathers experience and synthesizes it. Conclusions then spread in a clear, practical form. New and experienced staff both gain from that spread. The training arm exists to provide that system. Research by covert offices gets a coordination rule. Work on doctrine or techniques must be shared. Only single-division problems are excepted from sharing. Even then, use of the end product is claimed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100030017-8:
Official routing slip with a bundle of attached papers. The slip names Mr. Wilfred L. Peel as recipient. It came from an assistant director's office. A memorandum dated 8 May 1953 sits inside. That memo went to the Comptroller. The Organization and Methods chief got a copy. The Logistics chief and personnel chief got copies too.

Functions of two branches form the memo subject. The Central Processing Branch is one of them. The Passenger Movement Branch is the other. April 1953 memos are cited as references. One came from the Management Officer on 21 April. Another came from the Personnel Director on 24 April. Later text joins the two branches in one area. Physical closeness would ease traveler processing. Space layout should be designed for that flow. The processing chief schedules travelers toward the movement branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100019-8:
Report dated 21 March 1952 on intelligence coordination. The Office of Intelligence Coordination control office is the subject. Its Top Secret area office was reviewed for compliance. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote the report. The survey date was 19 March 1952. Uniform methods across the Agency were the review goal. The area officer and his deputy are listed.

Departures from the basic system are listed first. The office receives documents direct from outside agencies. It assigns its own control number to them. Its coordination function drives much of that flow. It reproduces documents and sends copies onward. A final document may bear several numbers in sequence. An IAC number and a fresh office number both appear. An example traces one State Department memorandum. It passed through the Executive Registry first. Each action by an area adds a new number. Continuity of control suffers under that pattern.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100190001-8:
Manpower survey of the Clandestine Services, Eastern Europe Division. A task force conducted the survey on Director's instructions. The survey report itself is dated September 1954. Postings and control of staff strength were checked. Reporting of staff within the unit was covered. HQ records on all staff were checked too. Staff agents and project staff were included.

Field staff sat beside HQ staff in scope. Data were taken as of 1 June 1954. Main findings of fact lead the report body. The unit ran over its total civilian ceiling. The excess figure is redacted in the copy. Its HQ ceiling was also passed. Reporting and posting systems fail a key test. They do not show actual strengths truly. Postings and locations of staff are misstated thereby. Senior Agency officials receive that faulty picture.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200020017-8:
Agency Procurement Office directive dated 13 April 1951 on procedure. The Building Services Officer is its subject. General functions are stated at the opening. All services to Washington area activities are covered. Requisitioning of supplies and equipment comes first. Expendable and non-expendable items both fall in scope. Transfer and turn-in of equipment are covered. Minor repairs coordination with administrative services appears.

Specific duties of the officer follow the general statement. All supply requests for his building come to him. He reviews and consolidates those requests himself. Requisitions are prepared by him from those requests. Turn-in and transfer requests also reach him first. Excess items are determined across his whole area. Transfer documents are prepared and coordinated by him. Delivered property is inspected and signed for. Form copies run to five for transfers. Stock number, name, and quantity list each item.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200060022-8:
Statement of duties for an Administrative Officer, GS-15. The post is Chief, Administrative Staff. Agency Logistics Office personnel work falls under it. Development of personnel and training requirements is directed. Records, programs, and policies for logistics are covered. Liaison with personnel files is maintained by the post. Training office support of those activities is linked.

Mail room and registry operations are administered too. Communications handling and recording sit in that charge. Space control and clerical support are administered. Messenger service and stenographic support are included. Records management for the office is supervised. Reports and forms control follows from that duty. Annual budget estimates are consolidated under the officer. Fund allotment and expenditure control is directed. Later pages give duties of subordinate posts. A mail and file clerk post is listed. A clerk-courier post is also described there. Special courier dispatch appears in those duties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200080020-8:
Proposals put forward informally by management analysts. Betterment of the staff program is their subject. Each proposal carries an action note beside it. Agency employees would detail to field hiring first. Two to three month details would speed the work. Permanent hiring officials would follow later. Civil Service lists would supply hiring officials too.

Lists for junior aides are named there. Referrals from all Agency staff are urged next. A steady referral path would be built. An Agency contest with awards is planned alongside. Hiring and security work would move outward later. Clerical and junior clearance would move to field offices. Vacancy lists would be simplified and cleaned. Accuracy of the vacancy listing is the aim. Staff should know all table changes at once. Many items carry a simple agreed action note.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200120025-8:
Memorandum dated 25 September 1953 to the Organization and Methods chief. A General Accounting Office survey is its subject. Punch card equipment and bookkeeping machines are covered. Electronic computers fall within the same survey. The Acting Comptroller General directs that government survey. Contact Division equipment is forwarded with the memo. That division alone in Operations uses such machinery.

An equipment list for the Index Branch is enclosed. All listed equipment is rented, none owned. Figures are stated as of 30 June 1953. Two IBM 024 machines head the list. Two IBM 056 machines follow in the table. Single 075, 077, and 082 units appear. Utilization figures run from sixty-two percent upward. Fiscal and finance work is described in the survey. Agency payrolls are prepared by machine there. One hundred eighty-one repetitive reports come monthly. Earnings records and object class accounting are included. Property and supply reporting closes the passage.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150013-8:
Part eight of the Agency indexing study accounts for gathering source items. Subject heading lists and classing systems were picked up. Other information for code work was gathered too. About six weeks went to visits in person. Places visited are each briefly described. Lists of items appear in an added part. Some items were taken for immediate use. Other items were noted for later interest.

Patent Office visits anchor the gathering effort. The Welch Medical Library was also visited. Johns Hopkins University houses that library. Both use IBM gear on classing problems. Indexing problems were studied at both places. The Patent Office stay ran about two weeks. Visits spanned 26 September to 11 October 1951. Machine indexing research there was studied thoroughly. Eight subclasses from Class 167 were selected. Medical makeups of matter form that class. Separate disclosures within patents were treated as units. Each unit tied back by patent serial number.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200035-8:
Notes on the Testing and Evaluation Division, Personnel Office. Structure of the unit opens the notes. It sits among the Personnel Office units. Military Personnel and Personnel Procurement are siblings. Research and Plans and Career Development are staffs. A covert Agency Personnel unit rounds out the chart. The unit's own table totals twelve slots. Its ceiling on 1 January 1952 was nine.

The chief is a psychologist graded GS-14. A secretary supports that office of chief. Development and Validation Branch holds three psychologists. Their grades run GS-13, GS-12, and GS-11. The Testing Branch holds a psychologist GS-11. Psychometrists graded GS-9 and GS-7 staff it. A clerk-typing post rounds out that branch roster. Present strength of the unit is seven. In practice it works as a single unit. Placement and hiring officials are its channel. Contacts route through those officials in performance. Field recruiters handle professional and technical staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100110009-8:
Paper dated October 1954 on briefing wives of overseas assignees. Other dependents fall within the same program. Briefing of Agency employees themselves is the parent effort. Three reasons require briefing wives as well. Wives cannot be presumed equally motivated for overseas life. The only safe assumption runs the other way. A wife may resent the ties involved.

Briefing must therefore build morale in wives. Sound motivation should be instilled by it. A sense of American missions matters too. Wives sit in a delicate position abroad regardless. Serious repercussions can follow from their slips. Inadvertent disclosure of information is one hazard. Much harm is done unintentionally by wives. Infractions of local customs can cause gossip. General briefing covers topics common to all postings. Motivation and morale head that general list. America's extensive programs abroad explain the commitment. Diplomatic, military, economic, and information programs are named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150081-8:
Study of the functions and duties of the Agency. The intelligence problem in the United States opens it. The Agency grew from World War II years. Prewar government did not lack intelligence at all. The State Department kept a wide information service. The Army and Navy kept their systems. Other departments picked up information and produced intelligence.

No joined system existed before the war though. On hand sources were not well used either. No central agency coordinated collection and production. National estimates lacked any putting-together home. Foreign policy shaping paid for that absence. Defense plan preparation paid alongside it. Power to coordinate receives close treatment later. Free-standing power to coordinate is not granted. Advice goes to the National Security Council instead. Final policy charge rests with that Council. Advising it is a main Agency duty. Matching national intelligence is another duty. Performing common services completes the main three.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220001-8:
Final report dated 9 October 1953 of a Legislative Task Force. It went to the chairman of the Agency Career Service Board. A meeting on 24 July 1953 started the work. A preliminary report followed on 13 August 1953. The Career Service Board considered it on 20 August. General policy guidance came from that consideration. Several legislative topics were set aside afterward.

Missing Persons Act proposals were not considered further. Home Leave Benefits proposals shared that treatment. Exemption from the Performance Rating Act joined them. The General Counsel's office took those items instead. A package bill might carry report items later. Other subjects were dropped as undesirable action. Still others were dropped as unnecessary legislation. Additional medical benefits head the dropped list. Job security receives a clear recommendation later. Tenure and separation legislation should not be attempted. Administrative freedom in those fields is worth keeping.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060088-8:
Printed as a blank form, a Personnel Data Questionnaire asks serving staff to record their military and schooling history in set boxes. Early sections probe present status: commissioned service, branch and corps, rank or rating, and serial or file numbers. Further items ask about National Guard membership and how the person entered federal armed service. Reserve standing, unit assignment, and any mobilisation assignment each get their own line.

Later sections turn to education, from grammar school through degrees held. The form is a data-gathering sheet rather than a narrative, and parts of the scan read poorly. Still, its structure shows what the Agency wanted on file for each person: service ties that could call them away, and the schooling behind the job they held.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090003-8:
A summary gathers the advice of the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Personnel on how the State Department should run its people. Its first call is for one flexible staff system covering nearly everyone under the Secretary of State. Department civil servants and Foreign Service staff would sit inside a single service. That service would start outside the normal civil service frame, though staff could still earn civil service standing.

Other points cover shared staff policies for all members and the special needs of service abroad. Extra leave, medical benefits, and living and quarters allowances are named as needs policy must meet. The summary also wants means for other agencies to lend staff to the service for a time. It reads as the blueprint behind a later State directive.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400160005-8:
Payment of travel costs from unvouchered funds is examined in a secret staff paper numbered SSI 1347. The writer works through the rules and rulings on travel status and on per diem payments. Attention falls on staff assigned to the Office of Special Operations and paid from such funds. The Director's power to order travel and approve its cost is a central thread.

Certifying officers, the paper notes, are bound to see that vouchers are properly certified and that payments match the Special Funds Regulations. Where normal proof cannot be shown for secret work, the paper seeks a lawful path that still guards the money. Parts of the scan are hard to read, yet the tension it handles is plain: secret travel still had to clear an audit trail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050015-8:
Retired naval officers and civil office form the subject of a Navy memorandum dated 16 September 1946. It asks whether such an officer may legally take a civil post under federal, state, or territorial government. Work for private firms doing business with the government is covered too. The usual cases, the writer says, are met here, though the statutes should still be checked in any single case.

One early point is that the question is the officer's private concern until he acts on it. An Attorney General opinion of 26 March 1897 is cited for that view. Private counsel, not the Navy, is the advised source of guidance. The memorandum was cleared by the Navy for release, and it reads as a careful signpost rather than a ruling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090011-8:
Quarters allowances for military officer personnel draw a General Counsel clarification built on papers from May and June 1952. At issue is section 5.7 of the Confidential Funds Regulations. That clause provides, in part, that once quarters allowances are paid to military personnel by the parent service, they count as basic compensation. The same clause appears in another part of the regulations, counsel notes.

The reading drawn from the papers is that an officer assigned to the Agency and serving overseas may draw his normal quarters allowance. A Personnel Director note of 30 May 1952 and a note routed on 17 June frame the request. The opinion sorts what the Agency itself may add on top of the parent service payment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140006-8:
Settlement of accounts of deceased civilian officers and employees is governed by General Regulations Number 104 of the General Accounting Office. A supplement dated 23 October 1950 eases payment of sums due certain staff who have died. Payment runs on vouchers approved by the agency where the person last worked. The supplement rests on Public Law 636 of the 81st Congress, approved 3 August 1950.

Under that act, all unpaid compensation due at death is paid to survivors in a set order of precedence. The order starts with the person the employee named, then turns to spouse and family classes. Speed matters in such cases, since families may depend on the final pay. The regulations give disbursing officers a clear path to close the account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140042-8:
A Comptroller General letter of 1 August 1952, file B-82514, comments to Chairman Olin D. Johnston on a Senate bill about missing staff. The bill, S. 1820 in the file copy, would let the government keep paying the salaries of civilian federal staff lost in the course of their duties. It also serves other purposes named in its title. The letter contrasts the bill with the Missing Persons Act already in force.

Under the bill's first section, the word person would reach officers and staff on duty in the continental United States or Alaska. Part-time and part-day staff raise a question the letter flags. Definitions of department are tested next. The letter is Congress's auditor advising a committee before the bill moved, in the careful form such advice took.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120015-8:
A termination letter ends one Agency agreement and starts another in the same envelope, with names redacted. The earlier agreement, dated 8 February, is ended under its Article 12, effective when the notice is received. A new contract is enclosed for signature. The stated reason is twofold: keep the person's employment unbroken, and fit the security needs of new duties the person is taking up for the United States Government.

The Agency stresses that the swap is not meant to harm, cancel, or break the continuity of government employment. Standing as an employee carries across the change of paper. An acceptance line and the signature of an authorised contracting officer close the letter. Such swaps let cover arrangements change without a break in service credit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800220158-8:
Aircraft owned by air carriers holding certificates of public convenience and necessity are listed owner by owner in a reference table. Alaska Airlines of Anchorage and American Airlines of New York open the visible pages. American Overseas Airlines, Braniff at Love Field in Dallas, and Capital Airlines at Washington's National Airport follow. Aircraft types and counts sit in columns beside each name, with Constellation, Boeing 377, and Boeing 307 among the types shown.

Chicago and Southern, Colonial, Delta at Atlanta, and Eastern Air Lines appear in the same order. The Flying Tiger Line of Burbank and National Airlines of Jacksonville close the first sheet. A second sheet runs on through Northwest, Pacific Northern, and Pan American. The list served staff who needed to know which fleets the certificated carriers actually flew.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020003-8:
Army Special Regulations Number 380-320-2, issued in Washington on 10 August, print supplementary agreements under the counterintelligence delimitations scheme. A contents list numbers the supplements one through five. The base agreement, published in SR 380-320-1, coordinates four bodies: Army's Intelligence Division, the Office of Naval Intelligence, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.

These supplements bind the counterintelligence investigative agencies working under that scheme. Each one adjusts who handles which class of case where duties overlap. Delimitations work kept rival services from chasing the same suspects or missing cases between them. The regulation is short and formal, a patch sheet for the larger agreement that divided the internal security map of the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020030-8:
A memorandum of 20 November 1953 for the Director of Central Intelligence submits two tabs on security law. Tab A digests the statutes on espionage, sabotage, and subversion. Tab B holds the Delimitations Agreement on investigations. Primary duty for enforcing those laws, the memorandum states, rests with the Department of Justice. Under presidential directives, though, the work of probing such acts is shared out by agreement.

The parties named are the FBI, Army intelligence, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. The agreement was signed on 23 February 1949. It gives the FBI all cases involving the categories assigned to it, including matters in the possessions other than Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands. Military jurisdiction over the armed forces is treated in the following lines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020102-8:
Disclosure of OSS information on leaving employment is mapped against a list of statutes in a short legal reference sheet. First cited is the bar at 50 U.S.C. 50 and 52 on giving national defence information to foreign governments. A note under 41 U.S.C. punishes letting an alien see plans. Photographs may not be published without the commanding officer's leave, under 50 U.S.C. 45(b).

Diplomatic codes get their own line: wilful, unauthorised publication of a code or coded matter is barred by 22 U.S.C. 155. Using papers to break statutes or treaty duties is covered at 18 U.S.C. 98. Other lines reach agriculture staff who publish withheld data, and patent secrecy in the national interest. The sheet is a checklist for anyone drafting a separation warning.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040001-8:
Congressional Record pages for the Senate in 1950 print debate and bill text on federal records and archives. Definitions fill the visible passage. Servicing means making information in records held by the Administrator available for use. That includes furnishing records or copies to government agencies for official use and to the public. The National Archives of the United States is defined as records the Archivist has judged worth keeping for good.

Unauthenticated copies are defined as exact copies that carry no seal and need not be taken as legal evidence. The passage belongs to the records provisions that travelled with the Federal Property Act scheme. Other pages of the long extract range across the Senate's business of the day. Page 11253 heads one sheet of the print.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040010-8:
H.R. 4754 reached the Senate on 9 June 1949 and was placed on the calendar as the House version of the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. Its aim matches the Senate bills: simplify the buying, use, and disposal of government property, and reorganise certain agencies. Section 1 gives the short title. The contents list then lays out policy, definitions, and Title I.

In this text the new body is called the General Services Administration. Contract settlement work of the Bureau of Federal Supply moves to it. So do the affairs of the Federal Works Agency. Records management and transfer of the National Archives sit in section 104. The act form, already passed by one house, makes this copy a step nearer law than a mere bill print.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070008-8:
Federal Communications Commission Public Notice FCC 51-304, dated 28 March 1951, states the rules for using telephone recording devices. It sums up Docket Number 6787, at 11 FCC 1033, where the Commission probed devices that record calls on interstate and foreign toll service. A final report came on 24 March 1947. An order of 26 November 1947 made it effective, changed by an order of 20 May 1948.

As changed, the order took effect on 30 June 1948. Recording devices were allowed on toll service, but only under set conditions. Those conditions aim to make sure every party to a call knows a device is in use. The long file copy prints the full statement and the rules behind it. Wire recording was a live legal edge for intelligence work of the day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070080-8:
A Federal Communications Commission letter of 15 October 1947 to Mr. F. J. Bailey at the Bureau of the Budget comments on changing Section 605 of the Communications Act of 1934. Bailey's letters of 26 August 1947 had sent over proposals from the Navy, War, and Justice Departments. Section 605 bars unauthorised interception of private wire or radio traffic. Wiretapping and use of what it yields are named as falling under the bar.

The section also bars phone and telegraph companies from revealing the existence or contents of private messages they carry. The service proposals, framed as national security measures, would make those bars not apply in named cases and inquiries. The Commission's answer weighs the privacy rule against the security claim, in the form of a budget clearance comment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020002-8:
Interior Department appropriations for 1953 fill a long committee text on funding for the department and the island territories. One passage laments the lack of organic legislation as a guide for judging the programs before the committee. Against that gap stand the United States' duties in managing and defending the islands. A trusteeship agreement with the United Nations is cited, along with the high cost in American lives paid to win them.

On the testimony heard, the committee recommends about the same sum as 1952 provided. It warns it will not entertain requests for added funds in the same way again. Added bill language aims to return appropriated money to the Treasury and to tighten control of the High Commissioner's financial operations in the Trust Territory.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020001-8:
Benefits under two health plans are compared in a chart made for members of the Government Employees Health Association in Washington. One side offers Group Hospitalization and Medical Service coverage. The other is GEHA's own present group insurance plan. Hospital services head the rows. The outside plan promises no dollar limit, with services covered in full for twenty-one days of each confinement.

Semi-private accommodation under GEHA's plan is instead capped, at local Washington costs of nine to thirteen dollars fifty a day. Meals, nursing, medicines, dressings, casts, and intravenous work are each marked covered or limited, plan against plan. Maternity and surgical rows follow the same pattern. Federal staff choosing cover for their families weighed sheets exactly like this one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030073-8:
Appendix C, marked secret, inventories the United States Government's facilities for producing foreign economic intelligence tied to national security. Nearly every agency, the Hoover Commission had shown, is touched in some degree by foreign affairs. Each therefore needs some knowledge of economic life abroad, shaped by its own duties. A Central Intelligence Agency survey, made under NSC Action 282, counted the field.

Twenty-four departments and agencies, the survey found, had need enough to collect and analyse substantial amounts of such material. The appendix describes each one's facilities and arrangements in turn. Read against its companion appendix on requirements, it gives the supply side of the picture. Planners used the pair to find waste, gaps, and work done twice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030091-8:
Coordination of intelligence collection activities is clarified in a draft State Department instruction dated 31 January 1951. It reaches back to an unnumbered confidential circular of 9 April in an earlier year on the same subject. That instruction's principles still stand, the draft says. Present circumstances, though, call for a clearer statement and a fuller account of how the government and the Department are organised for intelligence collection.

The Central Intelligence Agency, the draft recounts, was created by the National Security Act of 1947. Its role is a focal point for coordinating the intelligence work of departments with such duties. It also supplies common services that one body can best provide for all. The draft then maps the collection machinery abroad, where embassy staff gathered much of the raw material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300130017-8:
A Personal History Statement, Appendix I, prints the Attorney General's list of organisations each applicant had to check and sign against. The list was made under Executive Order 9835 of 21 March 1947. Under that order the Attorney General names bodies found totalitarian, fascist, communist, or subversive after inquiry. Bodies that back force or violence to deny constitutional rights are also named, as are those seeking to change the form of government by unconstitutional means.

The Abraham Lincoln Brigade heads the roll, followed by the Abraham Lincoln School of Chicago and a long alphabet of groups. Each applicant must review the whole list for certification and sign the last page. Membership in a listed body could end a federal career, so the statement was no formality.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000100050045-8:
Weekly Activities Report dated 8 June 1955, from the Chief of the Language and External Training School to the Director of Training, announces three courses. The courses begin on 22 June and run for ten weeks. The courses are Basic Country Survey courses on Japan and on China, and a course on United States foreign policy in the Far East.

Japan and China meet for three two hour sessions a week, and the policy course meets once a week. The report sets out the aim of the new Basic Area Training Program. The aim is a broad grounding in culture, institutions, geography, resources, art, and belief, so officers can read facts and trends in their local setting. Other items cover work with the National Security Agency on language schedules and a panel that turned down three candidates for the Armed Forces Staff College.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300004-8:
Public Law 679 of the 83rd Congress, approved 27 August 1954, is the act that amended section 22 of the Organic Act of Guam. The act began as H.R. 8634 and changes subsection (b) of section 22, cited at 64 Stat. 389 and 48 U.S.C. 1424, with committee papers following it in the file.

Federal rules calling for trial by jury do not apply to the District Court of Guam unless the Legislature of Guam makes them apply. Rules for charges by grand jury indictment instead of by information are treated the same way. Terms for government counsel in Guam cases are read as the Attorney General of Guam or a person named under Guam law. The act takes effect as of 1 August 1950, protects past convictions from reversal on this ground, and keeps the rest in force if one part is held invalid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300013-8:
Report on the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands covers the period 1 July 1950 to 30 June 1951. It was sent by the United States to the United Nations under Article 88 of the Charter. It was issued in June 1951 by the Department of the Navy, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations. The volume is large, with a foreword, a chart of the territory, six chapters, a statistical appendix, and a documentary supplement.

Chapters cover the area, the status of the territory, political growth and courts, economic growth, trade, transport, public works, finance, and taxation. Later chapters cover social welfare, labor, public health, and education, followed by petitions to the Trusteeship Council and its findings. The appendix gives tables on population, government, justice, finance, trade, housing, production, labor, cost of living, health, and education, and the supplement prints the trusteeship agreement and related orders.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200020031-8:
Paper titled Covert Personnel Contract Practice explains how the Central Intelligence Agency puts covert personal services on a contract footing, and why written agreements are the normal proof of what was agreed. The opening frames the topic as a matter of past and current practice. It is meant to give staff a shared view of the use, scope, and effect of such contracts, without proposing radical change.

Categories of covert people are named as staff agent, career agent, agent, covert consultant, and covert detailed personnel, and the paper works from those groups. Later pages take up pay and allowance handling, noting that staff with good contact with headquarters and access to forms should meet the usual steps. Where security risk is high, contact is poor, or help is lacking, steps may be eased and set rates used.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200220002-8:
Memorandum dated 4 June 1953 to the Project Review Committee, through the Deputy Director for Intelligence, is titled Continuation of Support to the Library of Congress and marked secret in the original. The problem is to provide an index by subject and area to open Slavic literature that holds information of intelligence value, so researchers can reach Soviet publications in United States libraries.

The paper ties the work to the Director's duty under NSCID 16 to build, as a common service, indexes, accession lists, and reference services on foreign language publications of intelligence interest. It argues that organized access improves research, letting a researcher find evidence that may solve his problem directly. A worked example traces a Russian author of a 1952 book on rust fungi of the Crimea. The paper links the topic to biological warfare interest, and a sum is sought for added copies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130001-8:
Chrono index for 1956 lists, by date and number, the papers that passed through a Central Intelligence Agency legal office in that year. Early entries in January include a concurrence sheet on a proposed incentive awards program dated 16 December 1955. They also include a memo on requirements and authority for bonding of personnel, a memo on copyright, and a memo on keeping civil service retirement status. A memo for the record on the Missing Persons Act is listed.

Entries run through the year in the same short form, naming the kind of paper, its subject, and any bill number where the item is comment on pending legislation. April entries include comments on H.R. 10368, a memo on legal authority for running vending machines, and several memos on the Agency building, its cafeterias, concessions, and transfer of property and land. The file serves as a finding list for the office's 1956 work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130074-8:
Comments dated 10 May 1956 on a proposed Agency regulation praise the present draft as a clear and concise statement in a complex and difficult area. The points offered are aimed only at clarity. Concurrence is not made to depend on any of them being accepted, and the writer flags two wording problems as the hardest to resolve.

One problem is the draft's use of overseas to include territories and possessions, while leave rules use the word only for foreign areas. Staff reading both together might reach wrong views of their entitlements. The other is the use of authorised and approved, which in government practice differ mainly in timing. A later point proposes shorter wording for extending an overseas tour: no extension beyond ninety days without the written agreement of the individual, reached beforehand, and based on operational need.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130164-8:
Memorandum dated 9 March 1956, for the Deputy Director for Support, reports a meeting of the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors attended on 7 March 1956 in Fairfax. The writer went, as directed, to hear a talk by Mr. Fisher on the Agency locating at Langley, Virginia; the item was set for 1500, came up at about 1520, and lasted about forty five minutes.

Fisher is reported as saying he had opposed the Langley move in the past, but the question now seemed settled. His concern was that the county take steps to cushion the impact. He spoke of a large building, heavy excavation, and hauling that should be scheduled so as not to add to traffic on crowded roads. Later speakers are summed up in brief, one generally favorable to the Agency and one from the Chamber of Commerce.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020003-8:
Tab B, titled Liaison with Congressional Committees, explains how the Agency works with the committees it deals with on a continuing basis. Liaison covers arranging testimony by Agency officials, furnishing information in answer to committee requests, and keeping the relations within the assumptions set out earlier in the report.

Appropriations Committees come first. Liaison there centres on presenting the Agency's appropriations requests, with the Comptroller working closely with Legislative Counsel and carrying the major share for the Senate committee. Each year staff are told where the Agency budget sits in the overall federal budget and how much is in each place, the budget being placed in various government appropriations for security. Later passages handle other committees and a printing office employee who had handled secret material for several agencies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030002-8:
Printed bill introduced in the Senate on 18 September 1950 by Mr. Kefauver, read twice and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 81st Congress, second session. Its title is to protect the internal security of the United States against certain un-American and subversive activities. It would also provide for emergency detention of persons who may commit acts of espionage and sabotage.

The short title given is the Internal Security and Emergency Detention Act of 1950. Findings declare that a world Communist movement exists. Its purpose, in the bill's words, is to set up a Communist totalitarian dictatorship in all countries through a single worldwide Communist political organization. The means named are treachery, deceit, infiltration, espionage, sabotage, and terrorism. The long text then sets up boards, petitions, and court review, with copies of a petition to be served on the Attorney General, the Board, and the person concerned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030011-8:
Memorandum to Walter L. Pforzheimer studies the effect of the McCarran Bill, enacted as part of the Internal Security Act of 1950, on the 100 aliens proviso. The proviso in earlier law allowed admission of up to one hundred aliens a year in the national intelligence interest. The question is whether section 22 of the new act repealed or altered it.

Legislative history is traced from Senate bill S. 1664 in the 81st Congress, first session, through S. 1832, introduced by Senator McCarran on 11 May 1949, with hearings from May through September 1949 and a committee report in 1950. A statement by Senator McCarran on the Senate floor is treated as the controlling factor on what fell within the purview of the bill. Substitute bills, the administration substitute and the Kilgore bill, are noted as containing no reference to the proviso, so their defeat proves nothing against it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070017-8:
Notice of Pending Legislation dated 14 March 1956, from the Legislative Counsel, Office of General Counsel, circulates an attached bill for comment on whether it is of interest to Agency activities. The comment section sums up the bill and the issue behind it.

The bill would authorise the Secretaries of the military departments to pay counsel fees, court costs, bail, and other expenses. The payments would cover representing, before courts and agencies of a foreign nation, persons subject to the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Whether civilian personnel and dependents are subject to the Code was not entirely clear, with cases in the lower federal courts and the Smith-Krueger case then before the Supreme Court. Later passages note status of forces agreements with NATO countries and Japan and the Defense practice of sending a legally trained observer to foreign trials.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100150081-8:
House Report number 2732, Union Calendar number 858, 79th Congress, second session, is dated 23 October 1946. It is the report of Subcommittee IV of the Committee on the Judiciary, made under House Resolution 430. A letter of transmittal from the chairman, Sam Hobbs of Alabama, to the Clerk of the House accompanies it, the House not being in session.

The subcommittee was charged to investigate the circumstances of the disposition of charges of espionage and of possession of documents stolen from secret government files. Findings in the portion shown note that in the agencies to which reports or documents were routed there was no real control or record of where copies were. A later finding restates the rule that a person charged with crime is presumed innocent until guilt is proved beyond a reasonable doubt. It also notes items found in one man's possession at his arrest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200060017-8:
Copy of the memorandum for the Director dated 29 December 1955 on congressional contacts, read here for its Priority I names. Senator Saltonstall had returned from a world tour. In the course of it he had gathered observations the Director should hear, and he stands second in the list after Senator Russell.

Congressman Zablocki appears in the middle portion of this copy as leader of the recent congressional delegation, including Congressmen Judd and Wigglesworth, which had just completed a world trip. He should be invited at an early date for lunch with the Director and a debriefing session. The closing lines add that Congressman Vinson should be kept posted on plans for the new building and on new legislation. That should happen as soon as the Administration position was clear on what the Agency would be permitted to seek.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100003-8:
Department of State instruction dated 17 October 1956, to all diplomatic and consular posts, concerns studies of the Mutual Security Program then in train. A group named by the President is introduced in garbled opening lines, with members drawn from banking, a university, labor, and business, and the President's letter to the group is summarised.

Terms of reference are described as very broad, with a progress report asked by 1 December 1956 and a final report by 1 March 1957. The Department had not yet been informed of any travel plans abroad by group members. Senate Resolution 285, quoted in an appendix, authorised the Committee on Foreign Relations to arrange its own study. The House Committee on Appropriations stated in its report on the Mutual Security Appropriation, 1957, that it proposed a thorough investigation of both the military and non-military phases in the next year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100021-8:
Foreign Service despatch from Manila, dated October 1956, reports CODEL Dworshak, the visit of Senator Henry C. Dworshak of Idaho. The Senator arrived in Manila at 1:30 a.m. on Sunday 7 October, and the day was spent in sightseeing in Manila and its environs, in the despatch's partly garbled scan.

He was accompanied by the USOM Director, the Embassy control officer, and the USOM information officer. The party flew in the Air Attache's plane to Clark Air Base. There the Senator was given a full briefing on the activities of the 13th Air Force by its commander, General Ackerman, and his aides, then an inspection tour. At his request he was shown both the good and the bad: termite infested temporary buildings forming most of the base housing and hospital, and a few modern permanent structures. A tour of the nearby city of Angeles and of agriculture extension work followed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010015-8:
