Copy of S. 3897 in its introduced form, with the bill number printed after the sponsor list rather than at the head. Mr. Kennedy introduced it on 21 May 1956 for himself and thirty others, and it was read twice and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, 84th Congress, second session.

The operative passage visible in the middle of this copy is the new subsection (b) added to section 216 of the Budget and Accounting Act, 1921. Department and establishment requests for appropriations are to be developed from cost based budgets, in such manner and at such times as the President determines. Earlier sections renumber section 201. They provide for balances of an appropriation or fund to be merged with the fund for the same general purpose for the ensuing fiscal year, constituting a single account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100050002-8:
Department of Justice order number 204-56 prints rules and regulations, Part 12, for registration of certain persons under the Act of 1 August 1956, Public Law 893, 84th Congress, second session. The Attorney General prescribes the rules under the authority of that act, and the text is given in numbered sections.

Section 12.1 defines terms. The act means the statute requiring registration of certain persons. Covered persons are those who have knowledge of, or have received instruction or assignment in, the espionage, counterespionage, or sabotage service or tactics of a foreign government or foreign political party. Attorney General, rules and regulations, registration statement, and registrant are each defined. Later sections cover what statements and documents a registrant must file, in the interest of national security and the public, and treatment of a registration statement found incomplete or inaccurate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100210004-8:
Printed bill H.R. 8499 was introduced in the House in January of the 84th Congress, second session, by Mr. Vinson and sent to the Committee on Armed Services. Its title is to amend the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, the act of 19 February 1948, cited at 62 Stat. 21.

Amendments rewrite exceptions to advertised bidding. Section 2(c)(1) is recast as a purchase determined necessary in the public interest during a period of national emergency declared by the Congress. Section 2(c)(9) covers perishable or nonperishable subsistence supplies. Section 2(c)(17) covers purchases otherwise authorised by law. It also covers purchases, in furtherance of small business, labor surplus area, or major disaster area programs. The purchases are from concerns that will perform substantially within such areas, under the act of 30 September 1950. Section 7(b) raises a figure from twenty five thousand dollars to one hundred thousand dollars, and a reporting duty twice a year is added.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670013-8:
Committee print of the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, 84th Congress, second session, dated August 1956. It sets out improvements in federal civil service retirement benefits contained in Public Law 854 (H.R. 7619). The committee membership is printed under Chairman Tom Murray.

A highlights table compares the retirement system before and after the 1956 amendments, split at 1 October 1956. It lists salary deductions, payments, and the general formula for computing an annuity. It also gives examples of annuity computations, the reduction for retirement before age 60 other than for disability, and the reduction to provide an annuity for a surviving spouse. One line gives deductions as six percent of basic salary. Further table rows in the middle cover refunds on separation, children's benefits after an employee's death, and deferred retirement terms for employees who move to posts outside the Retirement Act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670022-8:
Tab E holds H.R. 7619 as passed the House, placed on the Senate calendar 2 August 1955, Calendar number 1316. The act is cited as the Federal Executives Pay Act of 1955, and Title I sets basic compensation for heads of executive departments and other federal officials.

Section 101 fixes twenty five thousand dollars a year for the head of each executive department and the Secretary of Defense. Section 102 fixes twenty two thousand five hundred dollars for the Deputy Secretary of Defense, Under Secretary of State, Defense Mobilization Director, Comptroller General, and Budget Director. Section 103 begins the service secretaries' tier. A long list later in the act names single offices at a lower rate. Among them are the Treasurer of the United States, the Commissioners of Federal Supply and Public Buildings, the Director of the Bureau of Prisons, and the Commissioner of Social Security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670031-8:
Tab K copy of Senate Report number 2642 of 18 July 1956, Mr. Johnston's report on H.R. 7619 as amended, held in the Agency's executive pay file with the same Calendar number 2687 heading. Titles I to III of the substituted bill cover executive pay rates, Civil Service Commission organization, and classification of department positions.

A retirement passage in the middle of this copy treats immediate annuity. A change in the law would permit granting an immediate annuity where the employee is otherwise entitled, rather than deferring payment. Section 8 then takes up deferred retirement in detail. Under existing law an employee subject to the Retirement Act who transfers to a position outside it keeps no annuity rights, only title to a refund, regardless of length of service. The bill extends rights to such a transferee with five or more years of civilian service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690002-8:
Analysis of the Proposed Overseas Allowances Act of 1955, dated 14 June 1955, works through the bill section by section. Title I covers objectives, definitions, and general provisions: section 101 states the objectives, and section 111 defines terms used often in the bill, with two definitions fixing geographic coverage.

Continental United States is defined as the existing states and the District of Columbia, so statehood for Alaska or Hawaii would not by itself end territorial allowances there. The Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands is put under the foreign areas definition, since its conditions are deemed closer to undeveloped foreign areas. Employee is left to presidential regulations, and coverage is limited to civilian staff. Section 121 continues presidential rule making. Part D, at section 241, would extend storage expense authority to all agencies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200140001-8:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 11 April 1955, gives comments on bills before Congress on civil service retirement, reviewed for Agency interest, impact on operations, and advantage to Agency staff. S. 58 would let staff retire after thirty years of service, at any age, on a full annuity.

The memorandum calls S. 58 more liberal in some respects than the Agency's own proposal for accelerated retirement. That proposal would add credit for overseas service toward both service and age requirements. The benefits of S. 58, if enacted, should still reach Agency staff. It asks that the right to reemploy staff under sixty without Civil Service Commission approval be kept, and to be kept posted. Other bills cover the word detention in criminal investigation provisions, and S. 2375, which would loosen the Retirement Act on earlier retirement, survivor benefits, rehiring of annuitants, and coverage of short term workers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200230001-8:
Memorandum dated 16 January 1956 takes up S. 1875 and its House companion. The bill provides tax relief to members of the Armed Forces while they are held by Communist government authority or missing in action from a combat zone.

It occurred to the writers, the memorandum says, that it might be desirable to have a benefit of this nature extended to Agency people in particular. It would seem reasonable to make it available to all civilian personnel of the government. The attached comment of 3 May 1955 names Mr. Knowland of California and restates the bill's purpose. Bill text in the file suspends a stated tax rule for a taxable year within an unbroken period of active service that began before February 1955. It applies where the member served in a combat zone, as defined in section 112(c), after 24 June 1950, or was missing in action.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200320001-8:
Notice of Pending Legislation on H.R. 7000 tracks the bill to final passage. The comment, dated 23 June 1955, names Mr. Brooks of Louisiana and sums the bill up as providing for strengthening of the Reserve Forces. Tracking lines on the form list House Report 987, Senate Report 840, and House Conference Report 1335. They also list passage by the House on 1 July 1955 and by the Senate as amended on 14 July 1955, and Public Law 305.

The enacted text follows in the file: Public Law 305, 84th Congress, chapter 665, first session, at 69 Stat. 598, an act to provide for strengthening of the Reserve Forces. The very long file also holds hearing matter. Senator Thurmond agrees with Colonel Boyer of the Reserve Officers Association, who testified on 8 July for the bill, and calls it the most practical plan suggested so far.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200410001-8:
Notice of Pending Legislation on H.R. 4933 is sent to the Director of Logistics, whose comment is the substance of the file. The bill, introduced in the House, would permit state and local governments to tax the private interest in property, work in process, and inventories. The property was acquired by the federal government but held by its contractors.

The Office of Logistics considers that the bill will definitely raise the government's cost of obtaining supplies and services by contract. It will inject great uncertainty into state and local taxation of government contracts. The comment begins an account of the typical government cost plus fixed fee contract. The bill's preamble in the file speaks of products and work in process of manufacture for military security and the national defense. It also speaks of inventories whose title the federal government has acquired while manufacturers hold them under contract.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200500001-8:
A CIA legislative file on H.R. 6600 follows the bill through to enactment as Public Law 368 of the 84th Congress. Introduced by Mr. Kilday of Texas on 1 June 1955, it amends section 303 of the Career Compensation Act of 1949. Its subject is travel and transportation allowances for certain members of the uniformed services leaving service.

The act lets a member retired for physical disability, retired with pay after at least eight years of continuous active duty, or discharged with severance pay choose a home for allowance purposes. Dependents, baggage, and household effects may be moved to that chosen home. The file records House Report 967, passage in both chambers in July 1955, and the printed act with House report material on the amendment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210025-8:
An appendix paper titled 'The Radio Medium as a World Resource' treats radio as a worldwide natural resource. It describes the medium, once popularly called the ether, as a means of transport for messages and remote control signals moving at the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second. Because it exists everywhere, it is not confined to one country like some physical resources.

The paper explains frequency and the radio spectrum, and how the usable range grew from a small band at the start of the twentieth century. By international agreement the practical range ran from 10 kilocycles to 10,500,000 kilocycles, though research kept pushing beyond it. That workable spectrum, it argues, is the world's supply, drawn on for communications, radar, navigation, and missile guidance, and later pages turn to vacuum tubes and channel capacity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210034-8:
A CIA legal memorandum of August 1955 for the Office of Security analyses the Crypto Security Law, Public Law 533 of the 81st Congress, codified at 18 U.S.C. 798. Its stated purpose is to stop disclosures about the cryptographic systems and communication intelligence activities of the United States. The memo looks at the law's bearing on CIA and on Agency administrative practice.

It sets out the offence: knowingly and willingly giving classified information on codes, cryptographic devices, or communication intelligence to an unauthorised person, or using it to benefit a foreign government. The memo is candid that its legal points are not beyond argument. Its real aim is practical: it recommends steps the Agency, and to some extent other departments, could take to strengthen the government's case if a prosecution under the Act were ever brought.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100260002-8:
A final report of the CIA Insurance Task Force, dated 1 July 1951 and forwarded to the Director on 20 July 1954, sets out the Agency's new employee insurance program. The Career Service Board approved it on 30 June 1954. Contracts with the underwriting companies were in final approval, and two new plans, group life and group health insurance, were to be announced on 3 August 1954.

From the next day the improved program would open to all staff employees and staff agents. The body works through plan design, comparing benefit structures and printing schedules of payments. Its tables set out what a widow and children would receive at once, and the yearly annuity payable to each child, with caps tied to the number of children.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100270038-8:
A Senate executive document from the 83rd Congress sends two Paris protocols to the Senate. The President's message transmits them for advice and consent. Both were signed at Paris on 23 October 1954. One ends the occupation regime in the Federal Republic of Germany. The other amends the North Atlantic Treaty. It brings the Federal Republic into the alliance. The message went to the Committee on Foreign Relations on 16 November 1954.

The volume prints the Secretary of State's report. It also prints the full protocol texts. Added papers cover the Nine-Power Conference in London. That conference met from 28 September to 3 October 1954. Its Final Act is included. So are resolutions on the powers of the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe. The Brussels Treaty protocols follow. They deal with Western European Union forces and with control of armaments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030079-8:
A CIA personnel compilation quotes the leave and pay rules for federal staff. It draws on the Annual and Sick Leave Act of 1951. That is Public Law 233, approved 30 October 1951. Annual leave accrues by length of service. Staff with under three years earn half a day per pay period. Staff with three to fifteen years earn three-fourths of a day. Staff beyond fifteen years earn a full day.

Sick leave accrues at half a day per pay period. It may be saved without the yearly limit on annual leave. Up to thirty days may be advanced for serious disability. Leave for alien staff posted outside the several states rests with the agency head. Other entries cover pay rises under the Classification Act. They also cover limits on paying for unused leave, and the Assignment of Claims Act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200240157-8:
A CIA memorandum on special living allowances reviews a case involving seven employees. It went to the Deputy Director. The names of the men and the station are redacted. The office had earlier advised on the case. In a memorandum of 1 October 1952 to the Inspector General, it withdrew that advice. There was no legal basis for authorising the special living allowance. No valid justification appeared either.

An opinion of 14 August 1952 is also recalled. Payments above the territorial cost-of-living allowance set by regulation were improper. The area division had asked about other types of allowance before the special one was suggested. So there was every reason to know the allowance should not have been authorised. The file notes that money figures in both currencies are involved. It ends by asking for a full review of the case, and notes that the presence of one man makes the facts complex.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200250020-8:
A CIA legal memorandum answers a post differential claim. It went to the Deputy Chief of the Payroll and Travel Branch. The claim covers a period from October 1953 into the next year. The man was authorised to travel from Washington to a redacted post and back. His travel order first allowed 30 days, later extended by 15. He made four short trips out from his post, under the Chief of Mission or Station.

Before answering, the memo gives background on post differentials for detailed staff. It reports talks with the State Department's allowances staff. Foreign post differentials are paid under regulations issued by the Secretary of State. The memo stresses reading those rules with their purpose in mind. It also takes up how travel orders are amended. An amendment can fix the date from which a differential period runs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200300006-8:
A Civil Service Commission circular sets out a new reemployment rights program. It is Departmental Circular No. 869, dated 27 June 1956. It goes to the heads of all agencies and independent establishments. A companion circular, No. 870, ends the old system of rights tied to defence transfers. That system stops on 31 July 1956. The new program starts on 1 August 1956.

Under the new rules, rights are granted on a selective and temporary basis. They serve to staff essential work in critical or emergency conditions. They do not attach to every move. They may be offered as a recruiting inducement when staff cannot otherwise be found. Rights may be offered only under a Letter of Authority. The letter must cover the organisation and the named posts. Rights under a letter lapse after two years. Staff serving outside the continental United States get three extra months for travel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300010016-8:
A CIA Career Service Program package opens with the final report of the Working Group on Career Benefits. That report is dated 21 February 1952. A covering note of 19 June 1952 sends the Career Service Committee's final report to all concerned. The Director had approved it. Regulations and procedures to put the program into force would follow in the CIA Manual or in CIA Notices.

The contents list the program's parts. Tabs cover the career service boards and their functions. They cover a personnel evaluation report and an executive inventory. They cover selection and training of trainees for professional posts. Rotation and career benefits follow. An honor awards program is included. The committee's purpose, stated in its report, is to find, develop, and reward people with the skills CIA needs. It should motivate staff toward a career of service. It should also remove, fairly, those who cannot perform their duties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220059-8:
A CIA letter of 16 March 1953 comments on a draft executive order on security standards. It went to Joseph M. Dodge, Director of the Bureau of the Budget. The Bureau had asked for the Agency's views on 27 February 1953. One point concerns paragraph 9. That paragraph would have the Civil Service Commission keep a security investigations index. It would cover all persons investigated by any agency under the Order.

The letter suggests one addition. The chairman of an agency panel hearing cases should be able to administer the oath to a witness. False testimony could then go to the Justice Department under the perjury laws. It also questions the word 'consistent' in paragraph 8(b), which might be misread. Comments follow on single criteria. 'Knowingly associating' may miss the risk of a man who associates unknowingly. Intentional disclosure is named, but unintentional disclosure can also be a risk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240002-8:
A CIA legal paper studies how secrecy agreement breaches can be prosecuted. Its introduction limits the field. The sections discussed are those that could punish release of secret information of interest to the national defence. Two of them are the well-known espionage laws. Prosecution under those laws is limited by place. The breach must occur within the United States or its maritime jurisdiction. A breach overseas cannot be prosecuted under them, by citizen or foreigner alike.

The paper then sets out chapter 37 of Title 18, sections 791 through 798. Section 791 fixes the chapter's reach. It applies within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction and on the high seas. The paper traces that wording to a 1917 statute. It also flags one further provision, in the Internal Security Act of 1950. That section may have effect overseas. If so, a secrecy agreement could prove the defendant's knowledge that the information was classified.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240020-8:
A CIA legal paper gives further thoughts on seeking an injunction in a redacted case. It works from the contract theory. Its chief example is the Bliss case. There the government sued to stop release of information about certain designs. Its bill of complaint rested on two arguments. First, the release would breach the secrecy clause in the contract between the Navy and Bliss.

Five general principles stood outside the contracts. For those, the government argued a second ground. The Navy had supplied the principles. Their release would break the espionage law, then called the National Defense Act. It would also break Navy regulations. The court record is quoted at length. The paper notes a key distinction in the case law. A breach of the criminal law alone does not ground equitable relief. A breach of the government's property rights may.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100080003-8:
A CIA chart compares Basic School program accomplishments a year apart. The Basic Orientation Course is the focus. A year ago, responsibility was split between the Basic and Intelligence Schools. The course ran six or seven times a year. It leaned heavily on lectures, with one problem handled in discussion groups. The county fair exhibit had 20 displays from 10 offices.

Today the course is consolidated in the Basic School. It runs 11 times a year, with average enrollment near 90. Five lectures became discussion treatments. Grades rose at once in the first phase. Exhibits grew to 27, with 22 manned by the displaying offices. The Communist Propaganda Exhibit became an integral part of the course. The American Thesis now takes three discussion sessions and a special film. Management training also expanded, with a Case Officers' Administrative Handbook in preparation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100090002-8:
A CIA memo from the Director of Training to the Chief, Management Staff, takes up expansion of the Junior Officer Training Program. It answers a memo of 19 October 1955. The question of continuing the program was settled on 31 August 1955. A Deputy Director's meeting in the DD/CI's office decided to continue and expand it. OTR proposed a method and asked the Management Staff to work out the steps.

The method borrows from military practice. In a major command, some units sit below authorized strength while others exceed it. Internal adjustments keep the total within the ceiling. The same idea can serve the JOT Program, which benefits all major components. The proposal uses the gap between on-duty strength and the authorized ceiling. The DD/S, the Inspector General, and others agreed in principle. A meeting record of 12 October 1955 follows in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100010042-8:
An annual management improvement report of the CIA Medical Office is dated 11 August 1954. It went to the Chief, Management Staff, under a memorandum of 25 June 1954. The office reports no major problems beyond its own authority to solve. Its chosen areas for fiscal 1955 begin with physical and psychiatric standards. A major effort refines psychiatric and psychologic standards for Agency personnel.

The personal index evaluation has been revised. A register number system now protects psychiatric records and the doctor-patient relationship. The annual physical examination program is growing with help from the Office of Personnel. Machine-prepared rosters list personnel of grade GS-12 and above. A card index suspense system, keyed to birthdates, will spread the workload across the year. Later sections cover personnel surveys and medical reporting systems. Records now pass between headquarters and the field when staff transfer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030059-8:
A CIA file gives statements of functions for Agency components. The Supply Division statement comes first. The division receives, stores, issues, and controls Agency materiel in Zone of Interior depots. It keeps track of stock and of property in use. It ships and reships assets worldwide for operational support. It handles disposal of excess and unserviceable property. It also writes supply policy for the whole Agency.

The division sets stock levels from stated needs. It identifies and catalogs materiel and publishes the Agency Supply Catalog. It prepares budget estimates for its own work. A Planning Staff statement follows. That staff builds phased mobilization and war plans. Later statements cover the Printing Services Division. It runs the Agency's printing program and serves field stations, the National Security Council, and other approved agencies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040030-8:
A CIA paper, its first page missing, examines duplication around the Office of Scientific Intelligence. The surviving text opens mid-argument. FDD has an effective scientific and technical branch. Its exploitation work, broadly read, duplicates OSI's analysis function. The paper recommends moving that branch, people and functions together, into OSI. Better use of manpower and closer contact with trained analysts would follow.

OCI's military division also overlaps OSI. It covers military aspects of science and technology. Some overlap is clearly desirable. But speed alone, the paper argues, does not justify the present degree of duplication. OSI, TSS, the Materiel Board, Communications, and others all do scientific work with little coordination. Compartmentalization harms the effort. Later pages cover the Guided Missiles and Nuclear Energy Divisions. Their all-source coverage in depth is described, along with a call for more hard facts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410017-8:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 June 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. A USSR-versus-U.S. energy supply chart is complete for May. Radio facilities directed at the Bloc appear in first revision. Thirty charts show the range of effectiveness of radio broadcasts. USSR primary energy production and gas producing areas in 1955 are listed.

Many entries stand at proof stage. Bulgaria soils, smelters, mines, and industry sheets are in proof. Rumania's food processing and chemical industries are in proof. USSR copper and lead-zinc sheets are also in proof. A USSR automation program chart and military aircraft production charts appear. Later sections list due dates running through June and July 1957.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100470002-8:
An NIS production forecast covers fiscal years 1959, 1960, and 1961. It is dated 1 November 1957. A note says it supersedes all prior forecasts, whose copies should be destroyed. Parenthesized figures mark second and third revisions under the maintenance program. For each NIS area, the tables show planned production by year. Columns distinguish initial production from maintenance.

Entries list chapter and section numbers scheduled for each year. Some areas show initial production complete within the period. Others carry unproduced elements at the end of fiscal 1961. Section, chapter, and supplement titles are keyed to the quarterly production status report. The forecast is the program's three-year planning baseline.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490019-8:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 253 of 15 October 1957. Members received the tentative NIS Production Forecast for fiscal 1959-61, dated 14 October 1957. Final discussion was set for the next meeting. OBI review comments would circulate first. State proposed moving three Near East Chapter I areas from fiscal 1959 to fiscal 1960. Three other areas would take their place.

The other members objected. State's plan would load six Near East-Africa chapters into fiscal 1960. The committee re-affirmed the fiscal 1959 schedule. The order runs: North and South Korea, Albania, Greece, Ireland, Afghanistan, Israel, the United Kingdom, and the Arabian Peninsula. Dates run from September 1958 to May 1959. State accepted with a reservation. OBI staff visits to producing agencies were also approved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100010-8:
A progress report covers the Geographic Area, ORR, for August 1957. Its most significant point is continuity. Reports, photo intelligence work, and map library service ran without undue interruption despite vacation schedules. The Chief spent much of the early month re-briefing himself after six months away. The Cartography Division completed 97 maps and charts. Two Europe and Arctic maps were done on a crash basis for Mr. Stassen.

The Map Library Division received 3,013 maps and 1,051 related publications from foreign sources. Thirty percent stayed in CIA, 40 percent went to the Army Map Service, and 23 percent to the Library of Congress. The Reference Branch had its busiest August on record. It sent out 25,608 map sheets in answer to 1,356 requests. Outgoing communications hit a record 203.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140029-8:
A revised memorandum for the Department of Defense Task Force on Publishing and Distribution of Training and Educational Literature is circulated to members of the Technical Publishers Group. Much of the revision is legal groundwork. It quotes long passages from Howell, The Copyright Law. The passages cover what happens when the government itself infringes a copyright, and what remedy a copyright owner has.

The quoted passages explain the bar set by the Tucker Act of 1887. A damages suit against the government in the Court of Claims is barred for wrongs such as infringement. Government agents and employees, though, are not immune. A second part takes up the funds available for buying copyrights. It reprints Section 613 of Public Law 759, the appropriations act for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1951, as the current authority. The paper survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210058-8:
Legal review of a travel expense question fills a short Agency file from January 1954. An Office of General Counsel memorandum of January 20, 1954, answers a request for an interpretation of travel expense. The request is dated September 21, 1953, and was addressed to the chief of an administrative staff. A routing slip on the file records concurrence in a rewrite prepared for release.

The reviewer suggests one expansion. A paragraph on legal residence should spell out the features that make a place a legal residence. The cases in question involve staff posted outside the continental United States. They come back for temporary duty or home leave and then resign. Some resign at the temporary station, others at the place of leave. The point at issue is which travel regulations govern each case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100060001-8:
Routing of staff dispatches is the subject of a Records Integration Division memorandum circulated in the mid-1950s. A set of dated tabs is attached as references. The paper deals with how incoming dispatches are separated and sent on. It also covers overlaps in operational jurisdiction between area divisions. Those overlaps made a clear routing rule necessary.

Under the procedure described, most copies go straight to the addressee division. File copies pass through a central point. Experience with the method, the memo says, brought clear gains. Dispatches are more readily identified. Sorting and analysis are easier. Routing goes directly to the division responsible for the subject. The scan is heavily garbled. Names, dates on the tabs, and some steps in the procedure cannot be read reliably.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100140021-8:
A memorandum for the record dated December 20, 1955, documents a planning meeting. The meeting prepared a CIA briefing of the Foreign Service Inspection Corps. Agency staff met with Raymond C. Miller, the Chief Inspector. Inspectors Randy Higgs, L. C. Pinkerton, and Leon Cowles joined them. They discussed the proposed briefing to be given by CIA members.

The group reviewed the program given on January 19, 1955. They agreed to repeat several subjects. The subjects included the introduction and welcome, and the organization of the Agency and its overseas activities. They also included foreign intelligence operations and Agency inspection problems. Scheduling points follow. They include a fallback week in January. They include a suggestion that each speaker leave time for questions. About half the visiting group, Miller indicated, would be the same people who attended in 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200010024-8:
A memorandum dated October 17, 1956, goes from the Chief of the Finance Division to the Director of Training. It reports dissatisfaction with the training given to administrative assistants. Those assistants handle station funds and accounts. Renewed emphasis is expected on training assistants who will handle finance matters at small Class B stations. The division therefore argues that formal courses of instruction are now appropriate for such personnel.

Finance Division facilities had in the past been opened to staff heading for posts. At those posts they would take on financial duties. The recommendation goes further. The Agency's Office of Training should build a program for employees assigned to Class B stations. Those employees will be responsible for funds, financial records, and reports. The program should be a prerequisite for the assignment itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200020005-8:
Opening remarks by the Agency's Director of Training at an Office of Training correspondence seminar on February 25, 1957, survive as a transcript. The speaker jokes about the seminar's subject. It will be ably handled by those in charge, since he does not know what to tell the audience to do on it. He turns instead to the philosophy behind the responsibilities of the people under them.

He recalls a Christmas party two years earlier. He told the party that the change of the Deputy Director of Administration into a Deputy Director (Support) suited the Office of Training well. Later he warns against an old habit. Staff had underrated Soviet intelligence officers as boorish surveillance men. They proved to be area experts and fine linguists. The surprise at that was itself a failure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200150001-8:
A course report dated March 28, 1956, on the Agency's Operations Familiarization Course No. 2 goes to the Assistant Chief for Field Training. It was prepared under standing instructions for course reports. Thirty-five students completed the course; one dropped out at the end of the first week and another left at the end of the third. Thirty-seven students submitted critiques, and on the whole those critiques were very favorable.

The report draws a lesson from the first running of the course: every unit of instruction that students had rated poorly in the Course No. 1 critiques improved this time. The writer traces that gain directly to the use of student critiques in polishing the teaching. Quoted comments include a GS-12 officer calling a written exercise a good training medium, and a complaint that one test lacked precision of language.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300020013-8:
Weekly Activities Report number 44, dated November 6, 1958, from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School, records a week of people and programs. The school interviewed a candidate with native fluency in French, advanced fluency in Chinese, and some knowledge of other Romance languages. He lacked the qualifications for a staff job in the language program, so the school weighed him for a different assignment instead.

Other items note an invitation from the Office of Education to a conference on November 13, and a second French voluntary training exercise that its participants voted a rousing success. A November 4 meeting planned a film series to be announced in December and to start in January, showing one film in Russian and one in another language each week.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030003-8:
Weekly Activities Report number 41, dated October 16, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It opens with an accepted invitation. The chief would give a presentation at a staff meeting of division chiefs on October 23. It would match the one earlier given to Colonel White. The second item is larger. A delegation from the National Security Agency presented a plan. It would compile the most complete Chinese dictionary in existence.

The proposed dictionary would combine some fifty general and technical dictionaries. Production was carefully planned around IBM cards and inexpensive overseas research services. The school was told these would yield the reference at fairly nominal cost. A companion report in the file notes test recordings. French and Chinese versions of the A&E Staff's language proficiency test were being prepared for recording.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110004-8:
Weekly Report number 4 of the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff covers January 22 to 28, 1958. Its one significant item is a test-building job finished that week. The previous August the staff had been asked to help determine the equivalence of several forms of the Informational Reading Test used in the Reading Techniques Course. The decision was to rebuild the existing forms and add five more, making eight in all.

The last of the rebuilt tests was completed this week. Enough data was expected to be in hand by April to allow a first check on whether the forms really were equivalent. The report's tables then tally the week's assessment work: applicants, career staff, and conferences of the standard, special, and intensive kinds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400040017-8:
Weekly Activities Report number 41 comes from the Orientation and Briefing Officer. It covers October 8 to 14, 1958. On October 13 a briefing was given at the Army Intelligence Center at Fort Holabird, Maryland. Its subject was National Intelligence Organization and Functions. The audience was some sixty members of the current Associate Advanced Course. A program for overseas returnees followed on October 14. The dependents briefing ran in the same week.

The Agency Introduction program also ran on October 13, for fourteen persons. With the briefing officer away lecturing at Fort Holabird, a colleague conducted it. The report also passes on a remark heard at another school's course. Merging the IAC and USCIB into the USIB raised a legal question. Were Board members true members, or merely advisers to the Director?
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400090003-8:
Weekly Activity Report number 49 comes from the Agency's Junior Officer Training Program. It covers December 3 to 9, 1958. The Integrated Program, the chief reports, is progressing well. Trainee morale is good. The trainees' reactions to the lectures on the American Outlook almost uniformly matched the program staff's opinions. The staff attended the same talks. The office's reading of each trainee's capacity and interests was firming up as the course went on.

The week's counting is plain. Interviews were held with thirty trainees. That count excludes meetings inside the Integrated Program itself. Eight candidates were interviewed for the external phase of the program. Of five new files received, three were being held in suspense. They awaited test results and interviews. The rest were in process.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400100029-8:
Weekly Activity Report number 15 comes from the Agency's Junior Officer Training Program. It covers April 9 to 15, 1958. Its significant item is recorded for the record. It had already been given to the Director of Training orally. Every cleared candidate follows one path. He has been cleared Top Secret and brought to Washington for a pre-employment polygraph. Once his interview is done, he reports to the chief of the program. The chief briefs him finally on what will be expected, if he is selected.

The point is that there be no misunderstanding of the program's conditions. The week's pipeline numbers follow. Interviews were held with twenty-six trainees. Eleven candidates were interviewed for the external phase. Eight new files came in. Of those, two men were rejected and two sent for field testing. One was invited to Washington, and two were still under evaluation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100050009-8:
Notes on the Consultant Contact Week of November 2 to 6, 1953, were written for the record by the Chief of the Junior Officer Training Division. He wrote on November 9, drawing lessons from the visit. The consultants, the notes urge, should be oriented as soon as they are cleared. They should be told the shape of the program to come and why they were brought in. They should be encouraged to ask questions. Above all they should understand one point clearly. The program exists, fundamentally, to procure Agency junior officer trainees.

Scheduling is the rub. With a heavy first day behind them, the only time for such a session would be after five in the afternoon, or after supper. A second lesson concerns one speaker. He should have begun from basic ground. He should have explained why security matters, how operations get blown, and what the consultants could and could not do.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100003-8: A weekly summary report of the Office of Training lists the students then enrolled in its courses, sorted by school and course number. Full-time courses at Agency installations include the Basic Intelligence courses, administrative and counter-espionage courses, covert training, and clerical induction and orientation. A second section counts students in part-time courses. The scan is badly garbled, and most of the enrollment figures cannot be read with confidence, but the report's purpose is plain: a one-page census of who was in training that week.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200070006-8:
A speech transcript records an orientation course talk on the subject of training, by a speaker who leaves the detail to a colleague following him. He turns instead to the critique of the management and administrative courses offered for the first time in the previous few months. The students, he says, complained almost universally of one thing: the lack of communication up and down within the Agency. Communication, in his definition, means simply passing the word up, down, and laterally.

He warns against the opposite vice. Need-to-know and compartmentation, carried to their ultimate conclusion, would strangle training itself, and he is glad Colonel Edwards follows him to answer on that point. He closes by quoting the Jackson Committee report to the President on the need to improve training for national security work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300060009-8:
A memorandum dated September 8, 1954, asks a pointed question. Why are the Office of Training's facilities not used to the full? The memo offers recommendations. The writer had attended an August meeting of Agency division training officers. A point made there confirmed his own impression. Steps were in train to make attendance mandatory. The Clandestine Services would have to send their people to the office's courses. He treats compulsion as a last resort. The office should first understand the resistance.

The first reason he names is supervisors. A supervisor will insist that his clerk-stenographer can type, take dictation, and file. Yet the same supervisor does not require his officers to be trained. That holds at GS-11, GS-12, and above. They are not required to train for their assignments. Until supervisors demand trained people, he implies, classrooms will stay underused.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100004-8:
Adjustments to the Career Service Program are set in motion by a memorandum dated April 8, 1952. It comes from the Chairman of the Career Service Committee. It goes to the chairmen of its four working groups. The groups cover trainees, rotation, career benefits, and personnel development. The Director had asked for adjustments to the program. It had been presented to him in the committee's progress report of January 22. Each working group is to weigh the changes against its own part of the program.

The requirements spelled out include the gate to the career service itself. Participation requires employee or staff agent status. It also requires proven, satisfactory service. That service must be certified in writing by the employee's own Career Service Board. Proven service would generally rest on appraisal of at least two years of service with the Agency. Shorter service would need more to support it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100013-8:
Minutes of the fifteenth meeting of the Agency Career Service Board record the board in session on Thursday, November 19, 1953, at two in the afternoon in the Administration Building. Discussion opened on the DD/A board's paper about responsibility for the assignment and career development of general administrative personnel. A draft was put forward under which the component boards themselves would take the lead in registering their people.

Other business reached toward benefits and law. The board took up death and disability benefits, measured against standard government provisions with an additional sum proposed, and a request touching legislation that would permit more liberal treatment in personnel matters. The minutes show a young career service system still writing its own rules, case by case, in the autumn of 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400110002-8:
Personnel requirements for fiscal years 1953 and 1954 are called in by a memorandum dated May 26, 1952. It comes from the Agency's Director of Training. The call came ahead of the fiscal 1953 budget revision and the fiscal 1954 projection. Any change in personnel requirements was to be submitted for approval at once. Division chiefs were told to analyze their existing tables of organization and ceilings thoroughly. They were to judge how well current staff were used. They were to note what vacancies stood open, and whether position classifications needed revision.

Increases or decreases were to be shown as well. They might be driven by changes in mission, workload, or new projects. The estimates were due to the office's Administrative Officer by June 4, 1952. Attached material shows one live item. It is the two-week training block required of all clerical employees. A plan for clerical orientation before new staff reported is attached too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400120001-8:
A year-end report from the Intelligence School to the Agency's Director of Training sums up the school's second year. The school, formerly the Basic School, reports three things. It reports what it did in the year past and where it stands. It reports the major lines of work ahead. Three kinds of action took most of its attention. They were improving a going program of training, and building a new Intelligence School organization. The organization grew out of elements of the former schools. Developing its staff members was the third.

Plans for the near future turn on management of the school. The chief and deputy chief would divide their work systematically. Administrative detail would then be covered. Program development would get its share of attention. Staff replacements would be planned against long-term aims. Rotation and attrition would bring them. They would not be filled as gaps appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100140031-8:
A study of the Payroll Branch works through the branch's procedures in outline and then in detail. The outline lists its functional areas one by one: the handling of personnel actions, the central accounting work, reports, the form letters, and the payroll controls themselves. The detail shows a system built on a single slip. Every personnel action, permanent or temporary, was computed on a Payroll Change Slip pulled from the change slip file and sent on to the machine records unit under the usual controls.

One change is singled out. Actions were no longer bunched: the processing of the week's actions was spread across the whole period, so that the branch's workload stayed level through the entire cycle instead of peaking. Procedure instructions attached to the study give the full sequence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220005-8:
A staff paper on the Planning Staff of the Logistics Office describes a staff settling into its true work. Its function continues to be the overall planning of the office's entire operation. When it was established in March 1953, conditions forced it to do more. Conditions inside and outside the office made it carry functions of an operational and service kind as well. Chief among them was coordination. That work was then essential. It built the operating elements' confidence in the service the new Logistics Office could give them.

The functions that remain are planning in the strict sense. They include setting the standards needed in planning logistical support for Agency operations. They include maintaining a logistics library serving all elements of the Agency. They include assigning priorities under the Controlled Materials program when required. Branch statements below the staff's own fill out the detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100230022-8:
A memorandum dated August 11, 1953, goes to the Deputy Director of Training (Special). It proposes using IBM facilities to produce the Agency Office of Training's statistical reports. The Registrar's data on students was surveyed first. It covered the training request form. It covered the student rosters showing who had completed each phase of training. From that data ten items were selected. They begin with the student's name and the sponsoring office, down to staff and division. They end with the student's age.

The memorandum argues the equipment would serve more than student statistics. It was essential to furnishing those statistics. It would also make other Assessment and Evaluation programs run better. Not more than half its cost, it suggests, should be charged to the student statistics work. If the office accepted the expense in salaries and equipment, the plan was quite feasible.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200010007-8:
Foreign Service Personnel Circular No. 98, dated May 9, 1952, sets the rules for efficiency reports on Foreign Service personnel. It covers their preparation, submission, disposition, and disclosure. It sweeps away the earlier instructions. It names Foreign Service Personnel Circulars No. 54 of August 1950, No. 59 of November 1950, and No. 75 of July 1951. It names a circular airgram of July 1951. It supersedes anything else inconsistent with it.

The circular defines its term first. An efficiency report is a regular, orderly, factual report on a person's performance. Its instructions then work down the form. They cover the reviewing officer. He is usually the highest ranking officer in the rated person's direct line of authority. He must be personally familiar with the work under review. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300200006-8:
Briefing notes headed World Survey range across the globe in outline form, starting with Eastern Europe. Most Communist leaders there follow Moscow closely and work toward socialism at home, the notes say, with some exceptions. Poland's Gomulka keeps independence in fields such as farm collectivization and church-state ties but backs Soviet foreign policy. Yugoslav revisionism stays a prime target for Bloc attack, while state ties between Belgrade and Moscow remain correct.

East Germany is called the most exposed satellite, owing to Ulbricht's Stalinism, economic trouble, and Berlin as a window to the West. The Berlin section weighs why Moscow pushed to make Berlin a free city, seeing a drive to force talks on Germany's future. A Soviet bid to reopen surprise attack talks is judged a propaganda move. De Gaulle's rise in France is noted as the biggest Western change of the past year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200020009-8:
A companion version of the Africa policy paper, marked CFEP 568/1, gives the same recommendations for Africa south of the Sahara in near-identical wording. Farming again comes first: subsistence farming is the general rule, the typical farmer has no cash crop, and dependence on one crop for foreign exchange leaves many economies exposed. The tenure system, which does not recognize individual ownership, is said to discourage farm growth.

The advice given is to expand American technical help for agriculture as a priority, raising productivity and widening the crop base, with special attention to soil research and crop yields. Help should not be withheld over the crop grown. Closing pages argue that free world states should add economic and technical assistance as colonies gain independence. The two versions differ mainly in small wording points and their paper numbers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100020010-8:
A preliminary report dated 18 August 1954, sent to the Director of Central Intelligence through the Inspector General, reports a manpower survey of the Far East Division in the plans directorate. A task force, acting on the Director's instructions, examined how the division assigned, controlled, and reported its people. Headquarters records were searched for all staff employees and staff agents, project staff included, at headquarters and in the field.

Three aims governed the survey. They were testing how accurate and sound the many staff control points were, and counting staff who were unassigned, double-slotted, wrongly slotted, or paid at headquarters from unvouchered funds. Drawing lessons for staff handling was the third aim. One finding states that a regulation bars using unvouchered funds to solve office problems. Yet in practice people stayed charged to old field posts while doing headquarters work they had not been cleared for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100020029-8:
A survey plan for the administrative burdens of the Clandestine Services is set out in a paper whose head is garbled in the scan. Its stated aim, in the legible parts, is to measure the paperwork and related load falling on clandestine work and to limit duplication of effort. The study was assigned to the Inspection and Review Staff, which had earlier made a delegation of authority study in the same field.

The method is a census of recurring demands. Categories to be counted are administrative records and reports required on a set cycle, required meetings on administrative matters, correspondence and limits tied to administrative subjects, and evaluations of administrative work. By naming each burden class plainly, the paper frames a count of how much time clandestine staff spent serving the administrative system rather than their own work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100130009-8: A single table compares transit time to and from Army Post Office posts, with present times set against proposed times. Rows are individual posts, their names removed in this copy, and columns give minimum, maximum, and average figures for a set of trips, outbound and inbound apart. Many cells are garbled in the scan, so row-level figures should be read from the original table rather than from this text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100030006-8:
A tentative course schedule, marked working draft only, lays out a course called The American Outlook, part of a junior officer training program. The first day, Monday, 1 December, opens under the heading The American Heritage. A half hour of introduction covers administration, security, and aims. It also covers the link to other course phases and a two-week exercise. A note adds that library arrangements and first-day reading must be posted by the Friday before, or no reading can be done.

Talks and seminars alternate through the day. A lecture asks about the philosophy of the Revolution and the Bill of Rights. A seminar compares the American Revolution with the Communist Revolution. A second lecture asks whether the people are sovereign in the American political process. The seminar problem is to build the power structure of the United States from a civics book and a Communist account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100040023-8:
An untitled transcript records talks at a training gathering, opening with an introducer's remarks before General Cabell speaks. The introducer jokes that he does not make suggestions for what Mr. Dulles should say, since Dulles does not know that a certain book is required reading for every instructor in the Office of Training. He credits General Cabell with doing more than anyone to make the Agency conscious of the role of training, even if a five percent mechanism had to be used for that purpose.

Cabell is also praised for challenging the Office of Training to improve its product. A lighter passage corrects a story about being snowbound forty-eight hours in Dallas, which the speaker guesses must have been Ottawa. Cabell's own remarks follow, turning to supervisors and training: even in a period of tight ceilings, a supervisor should still release subordinates for the specific training they need.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100230002-8:
Paper IAC-D-82/7, dated 4 June 1956, argues the brief for United States Information Agency membership in the Intelligence Advisory Committee. Background reaches back to spring 1954, when the information agency asked the Director to study its intelligence needs. The study that followed, IAC-D-82, was approved in July 1954 in its key parts. Its findings included that the agency should have an intelligence organization of its own to make full use of community resources.

That study had held that membership should wait until its own recommendations had time to work, and the brief now revisits the question. The agency's primary mission is stated as work meant to shape public opinion and answer hostile propaganda abroad. Reporting from its overseas posts ran to about two thousand items a month, the brief notes. Yet its value against the agency's needs had been drawn on only now and then.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030003-8:
Attachment B reproduces a Department of Defense instruction, numbered 5200.1 and dated 8 July 1957, setting policy and procedure for the use of code words inside the department. Its purpose is stated first, then definitions. A code word is a word chosen from those listed in JANAP 299 and given a classified meaning by proper authority. The meaning guards intentions and protects information on military plans or operations classed Confidential or higher.

Inactive and obsolete code words are also defined. The first has been replaced by another word with the same meaning. The second belongs to a plan or operation that has ended, where the meaning still cannot be declassified for security reasons. A later section covers classification, downgrading, and declassification. It holds that during planning the code word and its meaning carry the same class, though the using agency may downgrade the word when a plan must be shared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030012-8:
A memorandum dated 1 September 1959 assesses what a Soviet aid deal with Ethiopia means. The Office of National Estimates calls the announced program a clear step forward in the Soviet drive for influence in the less developed world. With aid to newly independent Guinea, it is also a sign of growing Bloc interest in Africa. The key element is a development credit of 400 million rubles, repayable over seventeen years at two and a half percent interest.

At the official rate that sum equals about 100 million dollars, nearly as much as all American aid to Ethiopia to date. A trade agreement, a gift aircraft for the Emperor, a school for one thousand students, and hospital equipment for Addis Ababa are also included. The memo still expects only slow progress in carrying the deal out, and judges that no early, dramatic internal threat is likely to follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100020004-8:
A memorandum dated 23 January 1959, numbered DPD-0596-59, asks the Director to approve a new approvals procedure for the Development Projects Division. For four years, formal approvals of obligation and payment papers for CHALICE, formerly AQUATONE, had rested on an AQUATONE project outline of 7 January 1955. Other projects run through the Development Projects Staff used the same base. That outline held the writer's original grant of authority as approving officer and project director.

A paper approved on 12 August 1958 had given provisional approval to budgets for CORONA, GUSTO, and other projects on much the same procedure. The new proposal aims to cut slightly the volume of papers needing the Director's own approval. It also aims to improve the explanations inside those papers at field level, so judgment can be exercised on full information. A later section turns from committing Agency funds to a further step for cutting paper flow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100080152-8:
An index to general provisions heads a long contract provisions text. Articles run from definitions and changes through limitation language, variation in quantity, inspection, and responsibility for supplies. Assignment of claims, added bond security, and federal, state, and local taxes follow. Default and disputes get their own articles, and one article is headed Soviet Controlled Areas.

Labor and conduct articles include the Eight-Hour Law of 1912, the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act, nondiscrimination in employment, officials not to benefit, and a covenant against contingent fees. Termination for convenience of the government takes a long article. Patent matter fills several: authorization and consent, notice and help on infringement, filing of patent applications, patent rights, and reporting of royalties. Rights in data, marked unlimited, and military security requirements close the visible list.

Secret project outline dated 25 January 1954 proposes construction of an Agency Records Center to replace the interim centre then operating at Rosslyn, Virginia. Funds requested are 405,000 dollars for fiscal year 1954, on an unvouchered basis, and the outline notes the project had not yet been considered by the Project Review Committee. The General Services Office originated the proposal.

Legal grounding is cited from Public Law 754, which required each federal agency head to run an active program for economical, efficient management of records. Control of the new facility would rest with the General Services Office, since the centre formed part of the Agency records management program, and centre staff matters would follow that line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010008-8:
Memorandum from the Agency's S/TR branch states a continuing need for current data on freight rates and cargo handling costs in seaborne trade between European and Far Eastern ports. The data support the branch's transport intelligence research and other projects. Inquiries to official sources and industry contacts in Washington had shown the figures were not available there, so collection abroad was required.

Commodities and ports are listed in an attachment, centred on trade between northwestern European ports, including British ports, and mainland Chinese ports. A few other ports are added for coverage. The memo notes that shipping companies, stevedores, and freight forwarders keep detailed current records, and that single-cargo shiploads such as fertiliser, oil, sugar, or grain should yield cost per ton figures readily.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020034-8:
Agency memorandum of November 1956 submits S/CST requirements for Hungarian refugees. The items are basic rather than priority, but they fill real gaps on the Hungarian construction industry. Former skilled workers and supervisors, the paper argues, know parts of that industry at first hand and can best supply the facts. The questions are aimed at such refugees rather than at the Defector Reception Center in Germany.

Opening items target former officials of the Ministry of Construction and engineers or officials of the large construction trusts. They are to be asked about trends in the size of the construction labour force, the share of skilled workers, and wage rates. Later items cover hours, shifts, leave, and how construction pay compared with pay in other industries for like skill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020124-8:
Memorandum dated 27 August 1956 from the Agency's Transportation Branch asks for clarification of transportation statistics and terms in a statistical collection on the economy of the USSR, ORR 10134. The branch had reviewed the published figures and found that answers to set questions would make them far more useful for analysis of Soviet transport. Questions are tied to table headings and page numbers in the source volume.

Rail items ask whether operating length covers only lines run by the Ministry of Railways or other lines too, and how workers are counted. River transport items ask for splits the tables omit: freight and ton-kilometres for rafted timber, towed barge traffic, and self-propelled vessels, plus passenger traffic by fleet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020160-8:
Submission dated 19 June 1956 gives economics requirements for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List for 1 April to 31 July 1956, Latin America, citing Guide No. 164. Argentina takes the first pages. Items are marked retain or revised one by one, and one rewritten item asks for Argentina's reaction to a seizure of petroleum equipment, in wording partly garbled in the scan.

Other items probe Bloc interest in trade fairs, offers to buy surplus farm goods, and offers to sell capital equipment. A Dominican Republic item notes a report that the USSR had proposed setting up diplomatic relations and had been turned down, and asks for information on any such proposals from Bloc countries. Most other country items are simply retained.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020214-8:
Agency collection needs for Syria and Lebanon are dated 12 March in the scan. They answer an oral request from PP/ECD. Bloc countries, the paper notes, had been offering trade lures to Free World countries. The lures were meant to draw them into trade and investment with the Bloc. The Middle East was the chief target named. Four lines of work are listed. They are offers of credits, offers of technicians, supply of plant gear, and long term deals in goods that are hard to sell.

Named cases follow, for checking in the field. One is a textile mill from East Germany, contracted by a private firm in Damascus in late 1955. The mill may have been meant for Aleppo. The other is a dry cell battery plant from East Germany. A conference on it was set for August 1955, but its place is not known.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100070011-8:
Contributions from the Services Division to the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List cover Western and Southern Europe. The list runs from 1 December 1957 to 31 March 1958. The legible text centres on Soviet-linked insurance business in Austria. A Soviet State insurance firm in Vienna is described in the items. It is said to be the only insurance firm in Austria that insures shipments to the Bloc on a large scale. A branch office of the firm is noted as well.

Reporting is asked on the work of that firm. It is asked on other Soviet-linked firms that handle trade. It is asked on how far those firms are controlled from outside Austria. Later items turn to firms that act as fronts. They turn to trade finance channels as well. Much of the scan is garbled. The focus on insurance and on front firms is clear all through.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180028-8:
Minutes ED/EC M-231 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 15 April 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 17 April 1957. The agenda has three items. The first is Defense papers on machine tools and electric furnaces. The second is a Paris report on the CHINCOM meeting of 12 April. The third is a recap of the work needed to get ready for EDAC. Attendance ran across MDAC, Defense, ICA, the Agency, State, Commerce, and Treasury.

On machine tools, the committee took up the revised Defense proposal. Most members felt it had improved on the earlier draft. Electric furnaces drew a sharper split at the table. The chairman held that no case could be made on Bloc shortage. The basic study, he said, did not show the Bloc unable to meet its own needs for furnaces. Defense stood by its broader reasoning on the item.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180046-8:
Minutes ED/EC M-259 in the Agency's files, issued 30 July 1957, record the meeting at 2:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 23 July 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. Notes cover List II quotas for China, a Defense proposal to upgrade copper wire, item 3052, and Yugoslav tankers for Poland. Numbered items are the NSC and CFEP policy review and a work program to carry out paragraph 9 of the revised economic defense policy.

State reported its position on quotas and read a first draft of a work program for its proposed policy paragraph 21, to be submitted after rewriting. The chairman restated the case he saw against each part of that State paragraph and proposed how the rival paragraph should go forward to EDAC for decision.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180064-8:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-278, record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 5 November 1957. The meeting sat in Room 913 of the District National Building. The minutes were issued on 12 November 1957. Notes cover a progress report from the Ad Hoc Subcommittee on List Review. They cover a proposal to export generator know-how to Poland. The firm name in that proposal is redacted. The numbered item is a look at ED/EC D-123/1.

The subcommittee chairman gave his hope on the list review. The basic job would be done by about the end of November, apart from tag ends. He reported that only one piece of advice had so far been made in final form. Talk then turned to the generator proposal. Defense and Commerce had voiced doubts that day in Working Group I. Those doubts led members to judge the matter outside the committee's remit at that level.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180118-8:
Survey of East-West Trade in 1955, kept in the Agency's files, is the survey volume of the Eighth Report to Congress. The report rests on the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act of 1951. The survey covers the last half of 1955. The Superintendent of Documents sold it at the Government Printing Office for 35 cents. A letter of transmittal calls it mainly a factual account of East-West trade in 1955. The account covers volume, makeup by goods, and pattern by place. A review of the Sino-Soviet Bloc's trade position goes with it.

Country control sections follow the survey in the volume. A passage on France records new rules published on 30 December 1954 and 12 January 1955. The rules came into force that January. They cover imports, exports, and re-exports of set products. They are products moving under transit status. They cover the licensing of goods by destination as well.

General requirements paper for the Agency's transport intelligence mission opens with rail transport. It stresses the need for sound figures. Figures should be given in flat terms, or as a share change against a planned or true base. Traffic and working figures are listed in detail. Exact rendering of qualifying words in stated figures is stressed. A small shift in wording can change what a figure proves.

The paper is full on air and money matters. Air items ask for details on new aircraft types. Price and entry into service stand above all in those items. Plans for their use in world civil air traffic are asked for. Money items call for working costs and revenues, and for values of transport plant and gear. Capital, labour, and supply inputs are named. Gear lists are wanted, with output, import, export, and retirement figures. Data on working efficiency close the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120005-8:
Current Support Memorandum No. 625, dated 5 November 1958, reports improved Soviet civil air service. It is an Agency Office of Research and Reports paper. It is marked as holding code word material. It states the immediate views of its originating parts, with comments invited. The body of the paper tracks one change at Aeroflot. New aircraft entering the Aeroflot fleet would let the Soviet civil airline grow its work further.

Prestige sales form a second theme in the paper. The USSR might seek to raise the standing of its aviation skill by early sales of IL-18 aircraft. The buyers named are Communist China, Czechoslovakia, and the United Arab Republic. Since at least June, Chinese personnel had been in the Soviet Union for training. The training was in connection with the IL-18. In late August, at least two Chinese air crews were picked for flight training on the type.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120023-8:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 577, dated 7 May 1958, reports a Czechoslovakian civil defence radio network. A country-wide network, believed to have been developed especially to serve civil defence, had been in operation in Czechoslovakia since early 1954. Control ran from Prague, and from Bratislava for the Slovak part of the country, in the legible text of the paper.

The paper treats such networks as a natural step in civil defence planning. It notes, by way of comparison, that the United States had included in its own civil defence plans the recruitment of amateur radio operators and use of their equipment for emergency communications. Parallel development in the two camps is the closing point: both sides were building radio backups meant to keep working after an attack.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120050-8:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 546, dated 21 January 1958, reports increased building of air raid shelters in Bucharest. A November 1957 report from a Rumanian national is the source. It states that every enterprise and institution in Bucharest had been obliged to build air raid shelters. Some enterprises had already built theirs by then. The paper gives building detail for the shelters it names.

One large shelter is described in the paper at 131 feet by 92 feet. Its sides and top are of reinforced concrete in two layers. A 10-foot layer of loose sand lies between the layers. The shelter was finished in 1954. It has two underground entrances, and an entrance and air vent on top. Others listed include a shelter opposite the Northern Railway Station. That one sits under the Railway Management Building and holds 2,000 people. One more sits under the National Bank on Lipscani Street.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140003-8:
Planning paper in the Agency's files takes up the United States Exhibition in Moscow in 1959. It examines what the exhibition was for. Branches reviewing the draft purpose disagreed on that point. One reading held that the basic aim was not to stir Soviet consumers. The aim was to present a complete picture of the United States economy from a producer's viewpoint. The paper allows that this does not seem wholly the case. Consumer plenty in the United States plainly impressed foreign nationals. The exhibition's stress should reflect that plenty and variety, while still seeking a rounder view.

Concrete suggestions follow. A home workshop of power tools for wood and metal working is proposed. A lathe, milling machine, band saw, jig saw, sander, and drill press are named. They are cheap items showing work and leisure gains. Sporting goods form another wide consumer field for display.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200180009-8:
Minutes TSC-M-55 record a Subcommittee on Transportation session held 28 August 1958. The fiche filing date reads 18 September 1956. The meeting sat in Room 1121, M Building, convened at 1000 hours. An Army officer chaired the session. Members attended from the Army, the Agency, the Joint Chiefs, Navy, Air Force, OSD, State, and Commerce. An Agency secretary served the meeting. Names are listed in full in the minutes.

The chairman reported on a paper of the Transportation Capabilities Estimates Group. The paper covers the Soviet Bloc's military transport power. It deals with launching and supporting a campaign into the area between the Baltic and the Alps. The paper would be disseminated, he said. An Air Force member then described a division-wide computer program for fiscal 1959. He listed projects for the year. They include ground interdiction targets in the Caucasus. They include the effect of fallout on troop movement rates in the Balkans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100050079-8:
Memorandum dated 17 May 1951 to the Director, from the Acting Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination, reports a survey of interdepartmental committees in which the Agency had an interest. The survey tried to isolate the questions the Director cared about, starting with a simple one: do we know what committees there are? The answer given is yes, in three attached lists.

The lists divide the field by standing. One list covers committees where the Agency has primary concern, from either an intelligence or an operations standpoint, set up by the NSC, the IAC, or the Agency itself. A second covers committees the Agency sits on without primary interest, set up by other agencies. A third lists committees often mentioned that inquiry found terminated or in process of termination. A closing point accepts committee work as a coordination tool while keeping responsibility with each administrator.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100100163-8:
Intelligence Advisory Committee paper of January, the year partly garbled in the scan, circulates a proposed NSCID 16. It circulates material on an advisory committee on foreign language publications as well. The draft directive in the file turns on one duty. The Director of Central Intelligence would ensure the improvement of procurement of foreign publications. The publications are for intelligence purposes. That duty rests on the understanding set out in the draft text that follows.

The scan of this copy is rough, and the covering note is hard to read. The place of the papers in the file is clear all the same. They carry the community's draft language on foreign language publications into the IAC. The language goes there for comment, before a directive issued. The subject is central handling of foreign language material. The duties of departments to supply what they hold are part of it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100120026-8:
IAC paper IAC-D-78, dated December 1953, takes up NSCIDs 11 and 12. The two directives cover security of information and avoidance of publicity. A staff study is attached as Tab A. The study was built to support a Director's recommendation to the National Security Council. Agencies are asked to name a representative to discuss the study at a meeting at the Agency. The aim is that the IAC can help settle the problem, as it had when the directives were created.
