The problem is narrow and legal in the paper's terms. NSCID No. 12 is classified Restricted. That class became an unauthorised one under Executive Order 10501. The order took effect on 15 December 1953. The study notes the choices open to the Council: upgrading the directive to Confidential, downgrading it to unclassified, or rescission. The NSC Secretariat had asked for the Agency's recommendation on that single point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100160004-8:
Staff paper on a coordinated budget presentation for the intelligence community poses the problem. The question is whether the budgets of the government's intelligence activities should be presented as one statement. The statement would go to the Bureau of the Budget and to Congress. The National Security Act and the NSCIDs intend one thing for the IAC agencies. They are to work as a system, interrelated and interdependent. Budget requests ought to tie directly to the coordinated intelligence program.

At present, the paper says, no machinery exists by which that can be done. Present procedures provide only for single agency presentations. Practical difficulties are spelled out in the paper. Intelligence activities often cut across operational lines. So the funds that carry out a coordinated program cannot readily be picked out inside agency estimates. A common basis for comparing agency requests still has to be built.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200050069-8:
Top Secret working sheet in the Agency's files gives instructions for correcting a target listing. Five rules are listed. The first is to correct the spelling of city names. Where the target is a whole town, Complex is inserted, with coordinates for the centre of the town. Where the target is an installation inside a town, the installation's coordinates are given. Primary categories are to be circled, since primary and secondary categories will be separated in the listing. The last rule is to verify BE numbers for complexes against installations, and supply missing numbers.

A Far East targets list follows, running in alphabetical order with airfields marked AFLD. Entries include Alekseyevskoye, Anadyr, Aniva, and An-Shan. Later entries run from Khorol, Kitoy, and Klyuchi to Komsomolsk, which carries an airfield and a shipyard mark. Kraskino, Kuybyshevka Vostochnaya, Lushun, and Magadan close the set, each entry fixed by coordinates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400050003-8:
Report on Agency responsibilities for putting the Technological Capabilities Panel report into effect works through NSC Action No. 1430. One general item concerns the peripheral war problem. It calls for study of techniques and weapons technology. It is being carried out by a Weapons Systems Evaluation Group study and by a study under an Agency contract, due for completion early in 1957. Names in that part are redacted.

The implementation report on Specific Recommendation C.3 is left out of the document, with security reasons given openly. The next item, Specific Recommendation C.4, is quoted in the text. It calls for a broader look at intelligence data, or a new technique, for discovery of hoaxes. Its first step is a safeguarded National Intelligence Estimate of success in keeping secret the useful intelligence techniques. Later text refers to a clandestine collection program and to full use of intelligence advantages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100016-8:
Confirmation message in the Agency's files, cite Whiskey-0138, carries photo report No. 1399. Its date of information is 18 January 1958. It covers Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. Jordan items are brief. Zerka Airfield showed no activity noted. The Zerka military installation showed normal activity. Lebanon items list Beirut International Airfield with 20 multi-engine probable transports. Estabel Airfield was probably unserviceable. Kleiat and Metulla airfields showed no aircraft. Riyaq Airfield gave no information. A military depot at Aban was active. Tripoli Harbor showed 21 coastal vessels, 2 dredges, and 2 probable freighters.

Syria items begin partway through the message. Hama Airfield showed 5 Fresco aircraft and 17 trucks. It showed 1 Creek type, 10 unidentified vehicles, and 2 T-6 type aircraft. It showed 6 possible field artillery pieces and 2 MiG crates. El Quseir and Hmeimne airfields showed no aircraft. Palmyra and Qamichliye showed no activity. Sahl es Shara was serviceable, with no change and no aircraft. T-3 showed no aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500070073-8: A declassified CIA document without a surviving title. The nameless pages wait. Their story is kept. The archive holds the file. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Readers can find it here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600020004-8:
A confidential paper on coordinating requirements for collecting intelligence information anchors the file. It opens with a basic question: what counts as adequate coordination before a field requirement is sent out. The answer, it argues, rests with requirements officers in research offices and staff tied to collection managers, not with researchers alone. Their first check is simple. They ask whether the answer can already be found in Washington, in finished intelligence or in existing files.

Later sections point to tools for that check. They cite bibliographies, the Library of Congress monthly list of Soviet publications, and systematic work by the Foreign Documents Division and outside contractors. The paper then warns that national intelligence objectives guide priorities only loosely. A collection facility may have little ability to act on a given requirement when it arrives. The piece reads as internal guidance on avoiding duplicate, poorly aimed collection requests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600030021-8:
A paper dated 3 September 1954 reopens a standing question: should State or CIA hold primary duty for research on world communism? Before the 1950 shake-up that followed the Dulles Report, a loose group had let researchers share ideas, though it produced no studies. In 1951 the deputy director wrote to State accepting that the Department held this duty for all agencies. CIA's old reports office then stopped its own work in the field.

State set up a staff of about twenty posts for the subject. Budget cuts shrank it hard: the special staff never passed ten people and later fell to one. Area researchers still covered communist movements country by country. The paper reviews later talks with clandestine staff about meeting their needs, and weighs a shared statement of needs drawn up with current intelligence and estimates offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600150028-8:
A briefing paper for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, dated 26 August 1957, argues the value of U-2 coverage of Soviet targets. Precise target facts for strategic weapons are set aside at the start. The core claim is wider: Aquatone photos play a rare role in building national estimates. Those estimates ground major choices on national security.

Three Soviet strengths dominate the paper. They are the guided missile system, the long range bomber force, and nuclear energy production. Knowledge of all three still holds wide gaps, the paper states. Much of the current picture is fragmentary, and some estimates carry large margins of error. Defence plans and the vast budgets behind them rest on that shaky base. Cutting the error would shift both plans and spending. Later pages weigh the gaps strength by strength, starting with missiles and nuclear work, where they loom largest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020003-8:
A transcript records an orientation talk on coordination in intelligence work. The speaker is Mr Reber, Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination, addressing new Agency members. He opens with jokes at his own expense. One wit, he reports, read his office's initials as the Office of Intense Confusion. The office was in fact built to relieve confusion, not spread it.

Coordination, he argues, is like happiness or love: simple to name, endless to chase. The hunt takes up most of a bureaucrat's time. Later parts work through live cases. He cites a current intelligence problem where one service, G-2, leads for the whole community and for the Director. He also flags the strain that every agency runs its own current intelligence work. Gaps between weekly Watch Committee sessions need handling too. The talk runs long and informal, mixing humour with hard cases from daily practice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020021-8:
A speech on services of common concern opens with a rueful joke. A year earlier the speaker made an idle remark to Mr McCarthy about loose thinking on the topic. The price of that remark, he says, is the lecture now falling on speaker and class alike. 

An outline follows the spoken opening. It contrasts the single agency the Act's drafters might have built with the many agencies that in fact stayed. What the law supplied instead was a system, leadership, and room to grow. The key clause is the Director's fourth duty: to run added shared services that the Security Council finds better done at the centre. Later sections test that clause against practice. One part faults a directive on economic intelligence for failing to give a truly joined approach.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700060009-8:
A badly garbled scan fills the file, its letter forms scrambled across most pages. With effort, the text can be read as a review of how requirements and collection tasks are formed, and how they conform to the priority national objectives.

Points that can still be read repeat the review's main lines. Priority objectives steer production and collection without ruling them alone. Department work runs beside national work. Research gaps drive requests, and field committees help rank the highest needs before they pass to collectors. Later lines stress that collection strength rests on each facility's own powers and running. Because the scan is so poor, only the broad argument can be followed here; fine detail in this copy is largely lost to the reader.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070062-8:
A first yearly report of the Advisory Committee on Foreign Language Publications, dated 2 March 1954, goes to the Intelligence Advisory Committee for noting. The body was set up under paragraph five of NSCID-16, dated 7 March 1953. Its task is to help the Director carry that directive out. CIA provides the chair.

Three subcommittees split the work along the directive's own lines. The first field is buying: helping the Director join up purchases of foreign language works for intelligence use. Captured papers fall outside that duty. Work done includes a deal to list member holdings of Soviet serials. Area files for field buyers were also agreed. Later pages cover use of the material once bought. One deal covers Soviet non-scientific works: a CIA division will work through them in a set order, serving each agency's own needs while cutting overlap.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470016-8:
Minutes of the eleventh meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee cover a session held on 16 September 1955. First, the group's third yearly progress report won approval. It would go to the Intelligence Advisory Committee with agreed changes. Next, pending bloc shipbuilding orders were taken up. CIA would revise its paper with a finer country split in two tables, as the mutual defence office asked. Naval intelligence would add an amendment.

Boron substances as high energy fuels came next. A revised paper had gone round to members. If no views arrived by 21 September, it would stand approved. On trade in freed goods, State's research office was building a study from official trade figures. Later items gave Defence special charge of technical data work. A rerouting case on two ferro alloys sent CIA and Commerce off to probe further.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470025-8:
Minutes of the second meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 6 December 1954. The group met on 1 December. First came a report on the Economic Defense Officers Conference in Paris, held 15 to 19 November. Full accounts would follow in a paper series. Head gains touched enforcement, tighter controls, the China differential problem, and Soviet trade trends and tricks.

Field officers, the report warned, carry too many tasks. Economic defence gets little of their time. Heavy loads and thin briefing on the program's aims blunt their case with host governments. Most had not even read a key paper on East-West trade, so its lessons were lost on them. The acting chairman pressed how enforcement could be made to bite harder. Later talk turned to how facts move from CIA and State to action agencies. One past finding on that flow drew a formal refusal to agree from the Commerce member.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490005-8:
A draft of the third yearly progress report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee goes out under a memo dated 10 June 1955. The writer admits a flaw at once: the draft runs in story order, year by year, and may be too stiff. Still, it covers the most weighty work of the past year. To ease review, the guts of big topics might move into tabs.

Process fills the rest of the memo. An acting chief will read and mark the draft once members have seen it. A final draft will then be built. Talk on the report should wait till 30 June at the soonest, so late work can still be folded in. The report text itself weighs how economic defence facts get used. Gathering is only half the task, it argues. Facts must also reach action and policy desks in usable shape, as one case on Chinese buying bids shows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490023-8:
A reference report for April 1955, dated 29 April, sums up a busy month. The Economic Defense Intelligence Committee met twice. It probed facts on freed goods, checked the state of economic defence gathering, and opened a look at Soviet bloc strategic exports to the West. Research programming and a survey of the committee's own workings also advanced.

Back room work fills the rest. The executive secretary set up the 14 and 26 April meetings. He pushed on a fact sheet program and a COCOM downgrading project, and drafted memos for two offices. Reference staff fielded daily calls for papers from the export control files: allied control records, parent body files, committee and joint body material. Analysts lean hard on that service, the report notes. A new cable rule began in April: cables now file by date, class, and post. The old subject file for cables was dropped.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510002-8:
Minutes of an Economic Intelligence Committee meeting held on 11 September 1958 fill the file. The room was 1121 in the temporary M Building. Staff changes open the record. Lieutenant Colonel DeVoss joins as Joint Staff alternate, replacing Commander Hirshfeld, who is reassigned. Thanks go to Hirshfeld for strong service, shipping and transport among his fields. Leo Goodman of State joins the requirements subcommittee.

Past minutes then won approval. Later debate turned on how defence studies get assigned and checked. One proposal would add a fresh layer of control in the review chain. Members warned that such a layer would change the recent pattern of assignments for the defence committee's work. It would also slow reporting and hurt the character of the product. The record keeps that clash of views, with names of the wide spread of agencies at the table, from Agriculture to the mobilization office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050075-8:
A study dated 5 December 1955 weighs the use of boron substances in fuels. It opens with why boron matters. Its high energy yield makes it prized for aircraft, missile, and special weapon fuels. Boron powder in slurry fuels turns straight into more thrust and more range. Two boron compounds, in low strength, have matched or beaten hydrazine in rockets, tests show.

American work fills the next part. The defence establishment runs a wide program to widen boron fuel use. Most boron raw stock for fuel goes into powder for slurry fuels. Soon, military needs for set aircraft and missile programs should pass the whole current yearly output of 800,000 tons. The bloc's place closes the study: its chief boron deposits sit in the USSR, with some in Communist China. No proof shows bloc use of such fuels in live operations, yet no proof rules it out either.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200160019-8:
A report dated 18 May 1954 tells the parent body's executive arm how a new diversion watch net has run. The net covers 1 January to 30 April 1954. In the summer of 1953, agencies had reviewed their backing on diversion cases. They found the setup too loose and unsure. Follow-up was patchy, and joint action came late.

So a net of named officers was built, starting work on 1 January 1954. Aid, State, and CIA officers form its points of contact. Aid's officer keeps a steady check on each case as facts build and moves are weighed. He is also the hub linking intelligence and action desks. State's officer hunts signs of illegal diversion. He owns, or joins up, blocking moves that fit State posts abroad. Later pages weigh what good cases do: even a failed block can teach an allied land to plug the hole in its own controls that let the goods slip.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010002-8:
Patent Office papers in the file centre on a secrecy order. A cover letter from a service branch chief, V Pisapia, sends the applicant his copy. The order rests on Title 35 of the United States Code, sections 181 to 188. The applicant is asked to sign the receipt in person and send it back at once. Any change of address should also be reported.

The order itself is blunt. The application, it states, holds matter whose open spread would harm national security. The applicant, his heirs, agents, and lawyers are barred from showing the invention to anyone not already in the know. Even staff of the principals fall under the ban, bar those cleared to hold it secret. Copies of the order and its receipt form repeat through the file. Names and filing facts are blanked in this release, so the invention cannot be tied to a person from these pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010020-8:
A legal memo dated 4 November 1957 makes the case for patent secrecy power for CIA. It goes to the General Counsel. The goal is a presidential naming of CIA as a defence agency under the patent laws. Section 181 is quoted as the base. When a defence agency chief warns that a patent grant would harm national security, the Commissioner of Patents must order the invention kept secret and hold the grant back.

Terms are then weighed. The Atomic Energy Commission and the Defense Department already count as defence agencies. A grant may be held for a year at most in normal times. In a national emergency a secrecy order runs for the whole emergency, plus six months. Breaking an order can kill the bid, or bring criminal charges in flagrant cases. Four secret bids now sit in the Patent Office, the memo adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070014-8:
A file on the Language Resources Program opens with a memo for the record dated 7 May 1956. At counsel's request, a staffer phoned a Mr Silverman at the General Accounting Office. The query was one phrase in a Comptroller General letter of 12 April 1956. That letter touched cash awards under the Incentive Awards Act, and spoke of study on a man's own time and at his own cost.

Silverman's gloss was narrow. The phrase was dictum, tied to its own paragraph only. It set no limit on the rest of the letter, which dealt with CIA powers under sections 10(a) and 10(b). Word went back so drafting of the award rules could be finished. An April memo rides along: the chief of the language school marked, in red, the open parts of a staff study on language growth. Those parts could be shown to the Comptroller General to back the award plea.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150015-8:
A short memo dated 28 April 1959 sends the Director a manpower plan. L. K. White writes for the support side. Since the manpower conference of 16 April, he, Gates Lloyd, and Gordon Stewart have thought the matter through again. Three fields, they hold, hold all the room for cuts: how well work is done; how units are shaped; and what work is done at all.

The first field covers waste, overlap, and doubled effort. The second asks if a new shape could do the job with fewer hands. The third asks which tasks should be dropped, cut back, or changed. The three are tightly bound, the memo argues. One task force of very senior men should take them all at once. Split teams, or tests run house by house under each deputy, would waste time and yield less.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200037-8:
A staff memo dated 17 June 1954 maps the snags in printing counsel's rulings. Its author had sounded out half a dozen offices first: support, security, the clandestine staff, rules control, finance, and the print shop. The broad mood was keen. Two offices, security and the clandestine side, held back on one ground: risk.

The memo weighs print or no print head-on. For print: rulings in the open would ease work at the bench level. Men could find the law of a point fast. Against print: the same texts could be abused, and abuse breeds bad rule. Words would be torn from their facts and bent to new cases. The brief facts of one case would be skipped. Head-notes, if used, would be read in place of the whole text. A scan of past texts deepens the doubt. A great many, the author finds, state no facts at all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400030017-8:
A memo sends the Director a trimmed draft of the Agency's security rule. The rule's number is blanked in this copy. A June 1957 call set the trim in train: the deputy director asked the support side to cut the text to its bare bones. An Inspector General study of how security cases are run sits behind that call.

The rule's frame comes from the top. In April 1953 the President signed Order 10450, on security needs for state jobs. It spread one act's firing power to all shops: the Act of 26 August 1950. With the order came a White House note. The Attorney General would send each shop a model rule, to set floor marks for the scheme. The Agency's text bends that model in one way only, the memo says. It makes room for the Director's own firing power, and for Agency ways where they must stand apart.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050015-8:
A memo for the record, from March 1958, mines a fresh court ruling for Agency use. The case is Kaiser v. United States, a pact suit in the Court of Claims. His text, the memo says, may help the Agency judge what sort of shield claim to raise when its facts are sought.

The state claimed shield. The court held the claim well made. An agency head, it ruled, may judge the shield for himself. The state had fought a bid to make the court peek at the files first and rule on risk by its own eye. Reed's text ranges wider, the memo notes. The shield of the state against Congress, he wrote, is a point no court has yet ruled. A chief must thus lean on past course when he acts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400060023-8:
A dated twin of the NIA Directive ruling sits as copy three of three. It bears the date 2 February 1959. The ask is the Army's, in a letter of 20 January from General Richard Collins. A clip from NIA Directive No. 5, he bids, should drop to SECRET. The reply is no, on grounds that run as follows.

One clause of the clip does the real work: it deals out spy and counter-spy tasks past the nation's shores. That clause drove the old board to stamp the whole text TOP SECRET. The tasks have since moved to a live text, NSCID No. 5, reworked in September 1958 and held at the top stamp with a tight list. The top council, the memo notes, shares the old board's view of such task sheets. This sort of risk does not fade with age. The deputy for coordination was sounded and agrees.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100020024-8:
A routing slip of October 1958 ties a training report to a White House study. The Killian board — the President's own panel on spycraft — had asked the state of the art. 

Its counts match the house report. Two hundred fourteen classes in sixty-eight courses ran inside the Agency. Mean load was five hundred twenty-three a week. Tongue work grew while the rest shrank in the summer dip. Print tests went to near fifteen hundred staff in thirty-five tongues. Spoken tests hit eight hundred twenty-two, in nineteen. Cash prizes of about eighty-two thousand went to some seven hundred staff who hit set marks in key tongues and kept them. One sore point is spelled in this copy: chiefs can spare too few of their men for tongue study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100160016-8:
Proposed deletions and new definitions for allied export-control items are argued in an annex to Coordinating Committee document 3700.1. The first entry, numbered 1051, covers spar millers used in making aircraft. Because bloc aircraft production was shifting from military to civil types, the annex reasons that added capacity would serve civil planes first, and no key know-how or critical shortage was involved.

Forging hammers and presses follow, marked for deletion on the same grounds of mainly civil use. Metal rolling mills are also proposed for deletion. Aircraft, engines, and aircraft equipment are instead redefined, with care over radio sets already sold abroad. The reasoning shows allied officials weighing how much civil trade could be freed without aiding bloc air power.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100200002-8:
Revised pages for the international export-control lists, issued in French on 10 September 1959 as document 3300, gather the results of amendments numbered four through seven. The opening note lists what each amendment covered. One dealt with administrative principles, while later amendments touched single numbered items on List I, some of them more than once.

Delegations are told which printed pages the revised pages must replace in their copies of document 3300. An index names the pages affected, from early pages through annex material, with the dates each change took effect. One note requires that fitting controlled gear on new or used ships sold to the Sino-Soviet bloc be reported to the committee in monthly statistical returns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200020074-8:
Export of equipment that makes embargoed goods, sent to non-member countries in the free world, is debated in a Coordinating Committee record of discussion for 17 March 1960, document 3925. The German delegation had raised the case. Its question was whether buyers should have to promise that goods made with such equipment would not be sent on to the Soviet bloc.

Delegates gave their own countries' practice in turn. The United States welcomed the question and warned the problem could grow as new governments arose in less developed areas. Belgium reported that its exports of embargoed equipment to non-member countries were barred unless a guarantee against re-export to the bloc had been obtained. The record closes with a preference for studying each case on its own facts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200070015-8:
Schedule pages list goods put forward for embargo, grouped by trade category and tied to Schedule B numbers used in export statistics. Leather manufactures open the visible sections. Transmission belting, sewing machine belting, industrial belts, oil seals, packing, piston cups, and rawhide ropes all carry a recommendation for embargo, with used goods named alongside new ones.

Inedible oils and fats follow, among them neat's-foot oil, oleic acid, stearic acid, and tallow, again recommended for embargo. Rubber manufactures come next, covering synthetic rubbers, rubber cement, and rubberised fabrics and sheeting. Later pages reach heavy gear such as railway cranes and powered overhead travelling cranes. The schedules show how widely the net of proposed China controls was cast, down to washers and belting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110001-8:
Japanese proposals to delete items from the International China Embargo List are weighed in an intelligence evaluation dated 20 December 1955. The study comes from the Economic Defense Division of the Central Intelligence Agency's Office of Research and Reports. A commodity-by-commodity review forms the body of the work, arranged in the same groups as the embargo list itself.

Groups run from metal-working machinery and chemical equipment through transport, electronics, metals, and chemicals to rubber and miscellaneous goods, each with its own tables. The review reports that Chinese production of many items proposed for release had either not begun or stood at a low level. Industries named include metallurgy, construction, mining, and rubber processing, letting readers judge what decontrol might hand to Communist China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110010-8:
Continuation of a side-by-side comparison of export control lists, dated 24 July 1952, carries the work from item 14 of the Japanese list to the end. Japanese definitions sit in one column and the Coordinating Committee's China list with British supplemental items in the other. Remarks flag where Japanese coverage runs broader than the allied wording.

Fertilisers open this part, matched against nitric acid and named nitrates, with a note that the Japanese text is the wider one. Scientific and precision instruments follow, leading into communications gear for aircraft, infra-red and ultrasonic equipment, ionosphere recording apparatus, and jamming devices. Valves and metal drums appear further on, defined by pressure limits and capacity. Together the two columns gave negotiators a precise map of where the lists agreed and where they parted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000200010026-8:
Action proposed by the plans directorate on Inspector General recommendations about the Technical Services Staff is endorsed in a February 1958 memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence. The writer states strong support for one change above the rest. The Materiel Board would be abolished and replaced by a Technical Requirements Board.

As he understood the plan, the new board would gather the division chiefs and the chief of the Inspection and Review Staff, chaired by the chief of operations. It would work informally and flexibly, and the old board's secretariat and working panels would be dissolved for good. On a separate advisory committee, he parts from the directorate's wish to keep it, while admitting his grasp of its purpose was thin.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000400020005-8:
Comments on the Inspector General's survey of the SR Division are furnished to the Director of Central Intelligence, answering his memorandum of 4 July 1956. The division states that it gained from the survey itself. Talks at every level, held while its activities were reviewed, were useful in their own right, quite apart from the written findings.

Agreement with many recommendations is recorded, with reservations on others, and the comments stick to the recommendations and the facts bearing on them. The report is noted for seeing the division's tangled position: probably no clandestine element had more complex ties to staffs, divisions, and the wider intelligence community. Its tasks had grown in step with Soviet activity. One disputed point concerns whether SR reports carry a general reliability that a reader can infer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010220-8:
A May 1956 letter beginning 'Dear Fred' gives a departing detachment leader his first priorities on arriving overseas. Two tasks outrank all others in the writer's view: setting aircraft emergency procedures, and following up on aircraft and equipment maintenance changes. Both were to be settled in the first few months, before operations settled into routine.

Missing-aircraft procedure comes first and is broken into three steps: announcing that an aircraft is missing, starting proper search and rescue. Releasing information to the press, all shadowed by Soviet reaction to overflights. The letter then turns to a flame-out suffered on one mission. Skidding the aircraft to balance wing fuel, with long autopilot use, is blamed, and pilots are advised to fly by hand for a spell in every hour.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040047-8:
Keeping AQUATONE alive past 1957 is the problem in a memorandum from the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. Two questions need answers: whether the capability should stay in civilian, Agency hands beyond the end of the photographic season then beginning, and if so, on what scale and in what form. The existing organisation had been built for a brief, intense effort.

Long inactivity and postponed decisions had already hurt morale, the memo warns, and the organisation could not be held together much longer without fresh direction. One path converts it to a standby capability with rare, limited use; the other phases it out. Air Force thinking is noted too: that service had always expected the project to run no more than two years, with its assets passing to the Strategic Air Command the following fall.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200080025-8:
Flight planning procedures for AQUATONE, and how they were coordinated with Air Force headquarters and the Strategic Air Command, are reviewed in a 25 April 1958 memorandum. One standard practice is examined first: launching two aircraft together, so a backup can finish the mission if the lead aircraft fails, or so one can serve as a decoy.

The review leans against routine pairing. The U-2 had an outstanding record for reliability, far above combat aircraft. In about two years and roughly twenty-five true overflight missions, only one abort had occurred, late in a mission to Baku, caused by an inverter failure and costing little coverage. Other passages weigh how radar reflection changes when a route flies offshore rather than along a coastline.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110021-8:
Ground handling of satellite photos is planned in an ITEK proposal, number DSDP-58-9. The plan was approved by Walter J. Levison. He was general manager of the firm's Defense Systems Division. After talks with the using agency, a set of tools had been agreed for a first skill. Work toward a top skill was also agreed. Its design details were not yet fixed.

Three stages shape the program. First comes design and test models for a quick skill. Next come study and test models for the top skill. Last comes making of the final gear. The stages overlap to save time. Task details get exact. A contact copier would copy seventy-millimetre film at up to seventy-five feet per minute. It would set its own exposure. A further task covers the maths of turning photo points into map points.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200200003-8:
A United States reply to a Soviet protest is issued as a press release on 19 July 1956, numbered 398, for release that evening. The Soviet note of 10 July had alleged that United States Air Force twin-engine medium bombers from Western Germany had violated Soviet territory. The full text of the American note delivered that day is printed for the public.

The reply first corrects a phrase: there was no longer an American zone of occupation in Western Germany, so the reference must be to the Federal Republic of Germany. A thorough inquiry, it states, had determined that no United States military planes in or near Europe had made the alleged flights. The Soviet allegations are quoted in turn, including a claimed route over Brest, Pinsk, and Kaliningrad at a depth of one hundred fifty kilometres.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200260016-8:
A Bureau of the Budget official reports on a trip taken with Agency staff in a 17 February 1956 memorandum to Colonel L. K. White. He writes that he was tremendously impressed with the progress made on the special project. Rather than praise every success, he lists chances to improve matters that he had already raised orally with the project manager.

Operations plans come first. With the first phase of operations only weeks away, senior people inside and outside government worried that overseas plans were still not firm enough to plan logistics and personnel against. Even rough plans, he argues, should be given a firm basis. Local management authority follows: the project manager had already granted the local manager more power to act, and the writer supports pushing authority and responsibility further outward from Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200260232-8:
Special delivery of cables to a secret project's headquarters is requested in a 21 July 1955 memorandum to the Director of Communications. The project's rooms stood at 2210 E Street, Northwest, in Washington. The writer asks that cables come straight from the Signal Center to those rooms, handled by a small staff of specially cleared men, so knowledge of the project stayed tightly held.

Incoming cables would be delivered four times a day on a schedule still to be fixed. Three copies of each would reach the headquarters: one for the Director or his deputy when advisable, one for the central file, and one action copy for the proper project officer. Named action officers cover urgent traffic for administration, operations, security, and communications, with James A. Cunningham Jr. among them, and releasing officers are named for outgoing cables.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100020103-8:
Reviewer's notes on a draft paper, Project 34.1928, work through the text page by page and line by line, asking for fixes before the paper can go forward. One note records that forty per cent of the entire domestic production of machinery and transport equipment covered one set of commodities named in the draft. Another corrects the word 'autarchy' to 'autarky' and tells the author to check the usage through the rest of the paper.

Structural advice follows: material at the head of the draft belongs better as a foreword, and since the paper is now written, its tense should shift from future to historical present. Tables draw repeated fire. One table's totals do not make clear whether they show exports or imports, another lacks the 1956 balance. A third is said to need closer documentation tied to specific parts of the tables.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100030021-8:
Intelligence targets for the Soviet aircraft industry are requested in a paper dated 21 October, sent from the Industrial Division through the Aircraft Branch. Basic needs are set out first. Monthly production rates at each plant, past, present, and planned to phase-out, are wanted, along with development trends in major components of delivery systems and plans for improved or new weapon systems.

Documents, designs, and specifications of aircraft and parts are sought, as are factory markings, changes in factory layout and construction, shifts in the labour force, and sources and amounts of incoming shipments. Target locations follow, starting with two adjacent airframe plants at Kuybyshev that together form the largest single bomber production complex. An aircraft engine plant at Voronezh is also named, with a request for news of its current production.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050083-8:
Facts wanted on missile making at the Dnepropetrovsk Automobile Plant are set out in a paper dated 14 May 1953. The plant is known as DAZ. Fresh facts, plus a study of raw goods, point one way. DAZ is said to have made short-range missiles in series from 1950 to 1953. By then it had also become, in part, a maker of Belarus tractors.

Tight security at the plant is read as a sign. Missile work, most likely of advanced types, was still going on. Questions follow. Is the plant one site, or a group of separate plants? What did it make in each year from 1950 on? Were its workers sent away for special training? If so, the plants, dates, and skills are to be named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110031-8:
Research planned by the Economic Research Area of the Office of Research and Reports for fiscal year 1960 is presented to the Program Review Committee. The program reflects the Agency's broad duty for producing much of the government's economic intelligence. A directive gives the Agency primary responsibility for economic intelligence on the Sino-Soviet bloc, so the program serves the wider intelligence community as well as Agency needs.

About seventy per cent of available research time is expected to go to known and expected needs of the main intelligence consumers. Somewhat more than half of the effort goes to direct manuscript contributions to national intelligence estimates and surveys. Fourteen per cent is set aside for other consumers. Among the gap-filling studies planned is work on gold reserves of the Sino-Soviet bloc.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110121-8:
Comparing Soviet and American statistics fairly is the subject of an essay on what Soviet numbers mean. Soviet statistics, it argues, are not entirely false. The Soviet Union collects data not merely for propaganda but to run and control its economic plans. Falsifying reports at lower levels draws severe punishment, since central authorities need accurate figures for their own work.

Deliberate falsification is judged the exception rather than the rule, though the regime likes reports that show it in a favourable light abroad. The deeper problem is definitions: quantities are sometimes defined explicitly, sometimes by context, and sometimes not at all. Catch-up production figures also mislead, the essay warns, since matching American quantity can come at the cost of quality, style. Choice, so raw numbers are no sound comparison of short production runs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130002-8:
Polish aircraft industry sites are documented in installation sheets dated 1 January 1960. Each sheet follows a fixed form: country and town, installation number, alternate names, map coordinates, type of installation, a short description, the information required. A space to log reporting received in reply. Priority ratings mark how urgently answers are wanted.

One sheet covers an aircraft main parts plant reached by track from a main road, where components made on site were believed to be assembled into bases elsewhere. Questions ask about changes in production, the degree of activity and number of shifts, new construction, and a layout of the factory area, with photographs if possible. Other sheets cover a Warsaw site at Okecie and the WSK aircraft engine factory at Rzeszow, set on the bank of the Wislok River south-southwest of the town.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100190060-8: Declassified CIA material on gaps in information requirements for Poland. The blind spots again. The file covers the gaps. The archive holds the paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100050022-8:
A Soviet plan for long exchanges of technical staff is judged in a memo dated 26 September 1957. The plan had come from the Soviet envoy. It was sent to a subgroup on plant machinery and gear. Views were not all of one mind. The bulk of the group found a clear gain for the United States. That gain lay in the machine tool trade. A slight gain lay in car and farm machine building.

Net gain in technique, though, would fall to the Soviets. Exchange guests would in all likelihood reach facts of worth to Soviet trade. Set against that, American trade journals are open to the Soviet Union. They already carry much on American practice. True trade secrets do exist in the machine tool trade. Those secrets would need guarding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100270226-8:
Exchange visits between the Soviet Union and the United States are ranked for the Materials Division in a 22 November 1955 memorandum. Using net gain to United States intelligence as the test, exchanges in the chemical field and the nonferrous metals field would be among the most profitable. Petroleum and ferrous metals promise appreciable, if smaller, gain. Electric power shows a real but smaller net gain, and solid fuels the smallest of all.

Agriculture is left out of the rating, since its value was already established and future exchanges were being arranged. The rating assumes that Soviet delegations visiting the United States would gain little specific information not already in the open literature. Branch annexes, some of them withheld from this release, work the same test field by field down to the chemical industry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020105-8:
How the Office of Research and Reports writes its fastest product is set down in Procedures Instructions No. 1, dated 25 August 1958, from the Central Intelligence Agency's Office of the Chief, Economic Research. Current Support Memoranda are among the means by which the office supports the Director, the current intelligence office, and the National Indications Center on matters of current economic intelligence.

A memorandum of this kind must do at least one of three things: present economic intelligence current and interesting enough to be lifted almost word for word into current intelligence publications. Analyse a specific current development for signs of Communist intentions, or of factors limiting or easing Communist action; or analyse a general economic situation that could soon matter to national security. Style rules follow: four to five legal-size pages, triple spaced, written in either review style or source-comment style.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040077-8:
Pravda's review of the Director's testimony on Soviet economic growth is dissected in a memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence. The 28 November article, the memorandum judges, was published to make propaganda mileage at home. Statements in the testimony unfavourable to the Soviets were largely left out, while comments on the rapid rate of Soviet economic progress were reproduced in full.

Five specific remarks in the article are then taken up one by one. The first concerns the statement that the official Soviet index of industrial production understates output in 1913 relative to the United States. Pravda itself admits the force of a Soviet statistician's criticism of that index. A later paragraph defends the testimony as resting on the most comprehensive collection of comparative production data possible, not a biased sample.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040112-8:
Whether the Soviet state budget could serve as an arms control tool is studied here, round the 1960 budget plan. The budget most likely holds facts of use in any arms control pact. It could back up checks on the ground. In printed form, though, it lacks detail, even the detail a broad plan to cut arms would need.

A table gives the finest detail at hand, in billions of rubles, as follows. Planned spending comes to about seven hundred forty-five. Defence takes about ninety-six. The national economy takes about three hundred twenty-eight. Social and cultural measures take about two hundred seventy-four. Revenue runs a little above spending, leaving a small surplus. The study also puzzles over that surplus. Soviet finance writers call it a curb on price rises, set against bank credit growth. Yet the final surplus has repeatedly come out well above the planned one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040130-8:
Open Central Intelligence Agency research should go to universities, a memo to the Director proposes. The aim is stated plainly. Outside research groups and scholars should get some results of Agency study. The field is the economics of the Sino-Soviet bloc. Such help would aid their work on problems of national safety.

The idea grew from a meeting on 11 September 1959. The Director met the Senior Economic Advisory Panel that day. Panel members urged a change. Scholars who study the bloc should be able to use some Agency research. The research is broad and deep. Cleaned forms of key recent studies are the proposed path. Titles named include studies from 1959. One deals with rent policy effects in Poland. One deals with the ideas driving Soviet trade with the free world. One deals with economic aspects of Communist China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040202-8:
A draft timetable sends Agency research papers to review groups before printing. The papers are for fiscal year 1960. The groups belong to the Economic Intelligence Committee. In the first quarter, trade and finance takes two papers. One is on Communist China's foreign trade in machines and gear. One is on Yugoslav economic ties with the Sino-Soviet bloc since 1955. Minerals and metals takes the bloc copper trade in 1958. Transport takes China's reliance on foreign merchant ships.

Later quarters list trends in the Soviet economy through 1964. They list the bloc's role in building up the United Arab Republic. They list Soviet highway transport, and fuels and power in the Soviet Union in 1959. A caution closes the list. It was drawn up with no talks with the teams or writers who made the papers. It does not list all fit projects. It likely includes some unfit ones.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090018-8: Declassified CIA NSC briefing. The council briefed. The file holds the briefing. The archive keeps the paper. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090027-8:
An address by Allen W. Dulles before the National Association of Manufacturers was delivered in New York on 4 December 1959. He reminds the audience of an earlier speech. Twelve years before, on 3 December 1947, he had addressed the group's 52nd Congress of American Industry. His subject then, as now, was the Soviet challenge, framed as a challenge to prove that the system of free men under law can survive.

This remains true. Khrushchev, leaving the United States weeks earlier, had advised that Communism would in time take the country over. The 1947 Soviet hope had rested on the imminent collapse of free enterprise, not on Soviet industrial might. Stalin, Molotov, and Vishinsky had called the Marshall Plan a means of unloading excess goods to dodge an American crisis. The successors have dropped that thesis. Yet the basic strategy of world Communism, and its objectives, have remained remarkably unchanged since the death of Stalin.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090036-8:
A talk titled 'Significant Aspects of the Soviet Situation' opens with an unusual confession. Many activities of the Central Intelligence Agency must remain cloaked in secrecy. But its general management problems are not dissimilar to those of business. The speaker tells his Harvard Business School audience that the Agency trains senior officers in the School's Advanced Management Program. He hopes the link will be long lasting.

He jokes about signs of vigor in the room. They are surprising in view of Khrushchev's prediction that their grandchildren will live under Communism. Soviet propagandists were describing Khrushchev's visit to the United States as the probable turning point in East-West relations. Ilya Ehrenburg is quoted to that effect from 13 August. The talk later dismisses one sweeping claim about Soviet growth by 1970 as simply absurd. It warns that even more modest Soviet growth will free resources for increased military spending.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090045-8:
'Khrushchev's Challenge' is an address by Allen W. Dulles to the annual meeting of the Chamber of Commerce. He spoke in Washington on 28 April 1958. The Chamber counts two and a half million businessmen, and holds a key place in the nation's approach to international problems, he tells them.

Through Khrushchev, the Soviet Union directly challenges the United States in industry, foreign trade and aid, and military matters. To the slogan 'let us arm,' Khrushchev replies, 'let us trade.' The economic challenge is dual: goals for Soviet domestic output, in their words to get ahead of America in the economic race, and a program of foreign economic penetration. One case has the Soviet Union going ahead with a one hundred seventy million dollar aid program. It supplies arms under agreements worth one hundred million dollars. That raises the question of who the eventual user of those arms may be.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090081-8:
Khrushchev's Challenge is a declassified Agency speech text prepared for a Chamber of Commerce meeting on the peril facing the United States. It recalls how Soviet power spread across much of Eurasia after the war. Military action and political pressure were the tools of that first phase.

Since 1953, the speech argues, trade and aid had become a new weapon. Soviet influence moved outward through credits and goods, above all in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. The text then sizes up the Soviet economy, put at about 47 percent of the United States economy. Growth of six to seven percent a year is cited, with industry growing faster still.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090090-8:
Benson Briefing is a declassified Agency briefing aid on Soviet farming, built around charts that compare United States and Soviet farm figures for 1957. Its outline starts with farming in the years from 1928 to 1953. Collectivization began in 1928 and reached full swing by 1930.

The aid explains what collectivization was meant to do. It gave the state control of the food supply and drew capital for industry from the land. Collective farms owed set deliveries to the state at fixed low prices. Later notes track a shift in wording and policy, as farm output and housing gained a firmer claim beside heavy industry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100007-8:
The Soviet Economic System II is a declassified Agency lecture text on Soviet goals, capabilities, and limits for the years 1959 to 1975. It states the basic Kremlin goal in stark terms: the end of free society and a Sovietized world order. Methods may shift, the speaker argues, but that aim does not.

Charts compare output in key goods on both sides. One goal, matching the United States in a named good by 1960, is treated as already past. A later goal aims at nearly the 1958 United States level by 1965. Passenger cars show the widest gap: Soviet output is put at slightly over one percent of the United States figure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100016-8:
The Central Intelligence Agency is a declassified overview text that traces how United States intelligence work was put on a government-wide footing. It states that such work reaches back to George Washington, but that it was systematized only after World War II. A letter from President Truman dated January 22, 1946 starts the story.

That letter set up the National Intelligence Authority, served by the Central Intelligence Group. Both bodies are followed through their twenty-one months of life. Later pages take up the work and record of senior figures, among them service in Switzerland in 1945 tied to the surrender of the German Army in Italy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100025-8:
Soviet Economic Activities Abroad is a declassified Agency briefing outline dated 24 April 1959. It opens with the Soviet rise in rank: from seventh in world production to second in forty years, behind only the United States. Growth in the decade before 1957 ran at about double the United States rate.

Plans for the seven years ending in 1965 set Soviet growth at six to seven percent a year. Exports are put at 4.5 billion dollars a year, six times the 1938 level in set prices. Later notes look at oil, metals, and timber as rising export goods. They also weigh whether hard gold mining costs might push Moscow to earn exchange from goods instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020024-8:
An untitled working paper in declassified Agency files lists the questions an economic defense policy review had to answer. First among them: what should the aims of joint selective export controls against the Communist Bloc be, and on what basis should the control lists be built? Sharper questions on China controls follow.

The paper asks whether free world partners must all take part on equal terms. Ceylon and rubber, Japan and Communist China, and German interzonal trade are named as hard cases. It also asks how far United States controls should run past the joint lists. Curbs on imports from the Bloc close the list of open questions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100060002-8:
Staff Study No. 5 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 10, 1955, bears the title Economic Significance of China Trade to United States and China Trade Potential. Front pages carry handwriting that scans poorly, but the printed study is long and detailed. It forms part of the Economic Defense Policy Review of that year.

Country and goods sections fill most of the study. One passage weighs price against quality and reputation in winning sales. It estimates that one market's imports from free world nations might reach seven million dollars a year. A later section, on page 37, takes up control coverage for electrical machinery, apparatus, and appliances. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100110006-8:
Report and Recommendation on Measures Short of Terminating Aid, a memorandum from the Office of the Secretary of Defense dated 4 September 1952, addresses the Battle Act. An ad hoc working group had studied what could be done short of cutting aid off. Its aim was to make allied nations honor curbs on strategic trade with the Bloc.

Four measures are named as most workable. They are control of MSA counterpart funds, watch lists, offshore procurement contracts, and export licensing controls. The group urges that such steps be offered as gains, not imposed as punishment. Friendly nations, it argues, respond better to a chance of benefit than to a threat. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100150002-8:
Imposition of Financial (Blocking and Import) Controls vis a vis the Soviet Bloc Countries Other Than Communist China is Staff Study No. 10 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 22, 1955. Contributions came from the Treasury and Commerce Departments. At over one hundred thousand characters, it is a long and detailed study.

It weighs blocking Bloc funds and curbing Bloc imports as added tools of economic defense. Bloc goods sold to the West are described as goods aimed chiefly at Western markets. The study also notes that Bloc industry, run under rigid plans, needed outside markets to meet current needs. That need is treated as a point of Western leverage. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160001-8:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, revised draft of June 20, 1955. It opens with COCOM enforcement practice. The main duty for applying strategic controls, it states, had always rested with the nation from which a shipment sailed.

Early COCOM years gave enforcement little attention, the study grants. Later pages describe the screening tools that grew up in its place. A confidential check list, often called the Watch List, was used to screen export license requests. It also alerted Foreign Service officers to firms and persons whose deals might call for end-use checks. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200060047-8:
A clearance memorandum dated 11 March 1954, Control No. 1796 in its scanned heading, covers two reports for IWG members. Their information dates from January and February 1954 and from 9 March 1954. Sharing rights differ by post: some offices get the reports for action, others for information only, each at a stated secrecy level.

One note tries to fix the identity of a Popov tied to Etablissement Pfeffer of Vaduz, Liechtenstein. A Belgrade report of February 1954 is then taken up. It concerns a British firm's license request to ship 3,400 tons of copper to a Yugoslav firm named Progress. The copper would go in varied forms. A promise backed the request: the copper would not be re-exported. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040022-8:
Report on Monitoring a Basic Course is a declassified Agency memorandum from an observer who sat through the course for five days in October. Only three students took it: one from TSD, one from NE, and the observer, from the training office itself. Each came with a different need for the skill taught.

The chief instructor earns high praise for drive and care in running the course. Weak points are still named. Lesson plans for the course needed finishing, and help was urged to get that done. A further rule is proposed: if a class grows past four students, an added qualified assistant instructor should be on hand, since the skill demands near constant attention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040031-8:
Training Report is a set of student reports from Instructional Techniques Course No. 49, held in September 1960 with six students. The course had two stated aims. Students were to gain a grasp of how learning works, and then to apply those rules in real teaching practice.

Class work covered planning, clear speaking, drill methods, and the use of questions. Training aids and the testing of teaching were also taken up, though only at a first level given the short span. Each student gave a sample talk and drill session in his own subject. Classmates and the instructor then critiqued and rated the work, and about half the course time went to such practice. The report survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040095-8:
Training Report Forms is a declassified Agency memorandum on a bid to simplify how student results were reported. A survey report on the AE Staff had sparked the effort months before. The training office was asked to build a one page form for reporting any single student's achievement in any course.

Trial reports were drafted for a few set courses and sent to school chiefs for comment. Supervisors found the trials well done and useful. Yet the review lands on a caution: a short added narrative is still needed for a true picture. Strengths, weak points, discussion work, and skill in speech or writing all call for words, not boxes alone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00313a000500010062-8: This declassified CIA document covers security protection of ultrasensitive intelligence collection. The guarded take. The file holds the reference. The record stays. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add detail to the Cold War story.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 8 of Richardson's novel in letters is a volume of packets and last messages. Clarissa sends Miss Howe a large packet of letters, though not all she has received, for her family's sake. She confirms Mr. Belford as her executor and points to her papers for her justification.

Her uncle Antony's letter is more taunting than the rest, and her answer closes with a prayer for the whole family's happiness. Mrs. Norton writes of her cousin Morden's arrival in England. Clarissa fears Morden will be set against her, or worse, will seek to avenge her. Lovelace, in his own letters, lies extremely ill, with a clergyman praying at his bedside.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-8:
For books sixty-one through seventy, the full text of Dio Cassius is lost. His history comes down in the shortened form made by Xiphilinus, a Byzantine monk. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation prints that epitome in this eighth volume. The years run from Nero to the reign of Trajan.

Nero's fall, the year of four emperors, and the Flavian house pass in quick, sharp scenes. The Jewish war and the reigns of Titus and Domitian follow, then Nerva and the start of Trajan. Even cut down, Dio stays a main source for the first century of emperors. The volume shows how much a good epitome can save.
doe-osti-17120794-analysis-of-the-1-404-:
Sydney Coil, Rene Reifarth, Aaron Couture, and a Los Alamos team measured how krypton 84 captures neutrons at one sharp resonance, in a report issued 30 September 2026. The DANCE detector array caught capture gamma rays by time of flight, sorting events by neutron energy. The work feeds s process models, the slow neutron capture chain that builds heavy elements in stars.

Captures can leave krypton 85 in its ground state or in a longer lived isomeric state, and the split between them matters at a key branch point. For the s wave resonance at 1.404 kiloelectronvolts, the ground state share of total captures came out at 0.195, plus or minus 0.015. That value agrees well with results reported at other energies, the authors note.
doe-osti-2997987-fy24-fy25-efforts-to-re:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/80, by Matthew Bucknor, Sari Alkhatib, and Dennis Henneke, recounts two years of work to revive a dormant safety standard. ANS-54.8 covers fire protection against liquid metal fires in liquid metal reactor plants. Most sodium reactor standards sit withdrawn or inactive, even as new sodium designs head toward licensing and need shared rules.

A two-stage reinstatement and revision plan won approval from the standards committee in June 2024 and from the ANS Standards Board that July. The working group held its first meeting in August 2024. A project implementation plan was drafted, submitted, and approved by September 2024. The report logs those steps and the road ahead, giving designers and regulators a dated record of the standard's return.
dual-control-ship-s-company-part-8:
W. W. Jacobs sets a courtship farce in Dual Control, part eight of his Ship's Company tales. Mr. Culpepper, a retired sailor, coaches young Albert Sharp on how to win his daughter Florrie. Girls do not like steady young men, Culpepper warns; Sharp should cheek her a bit and show some spirit, since Florrie will not talk to a lad who will not talk back.

Culpepper's own marriage is his lesson book. His wife thought him steady and good-looking, with chestnut hair; she kept a piece of it for thirty years, then burnt it after a quarrel of words. A snug supper party, with roast beef carved at the table and ale passed round, lets Sharp try his new boldness under the old man's eye. Jacobs keeps his shore folk dry, sly, and fond under the teasing.
froude-history-england-vol-8:
Elizabeth's middle years steady England in the eighth volume of Froude's History, from 1856. The Protestant settlement takes firmer root across the realm. Drake and the sea dogs rise to fame on daring voyages and raids against Spain.

Froude writes the fifteen seventies and eighties with stirring pace. England finds its footing as a sea power and a Protestant state. Courtiers, sailors, and settlers all advance his broad national tale. The volume bridges the plot-haunted early reign and the Armada crisis ahead, showing a kingdom growing in wealth, confidence, and reach under its watchful queen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-8:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes for the afternoon of July 17, 1945, record debate on Britain's part in the Japan war. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Sir Alan Brooke led for the British Chiefs of Staff.

The chiefs first approved the conclusions of their 193rd meeting. Brooke then took up the British contribution papers, numbers 889 and 889/1. He said his chiefs were very pleased with the U.S. answer. The U.S. Chiefs agreed in principle to a British Commonwealth land force in the war's final phase. That agreement hung on settling operational problems with the U.S. Pacific commanders. It also hung on clarifying certain factors, which Brooke then proposed to deal with point by point.
gao-gaoreports-b-294358-8:
University Research Company returns in companion files B-294358.8 through B-294358.10, dated April 6, 2006. The same Health Information Network contract was at stake, after a court-ordered review of reproduction costs. GAO denied the protest. The agency had fairly kept its earlier scores when the fix was limited to revised offers on reproduction services alone. That approach matched the evaluation scheme in the solicitation.

A second point defends an upward adjustment to the protester's own stated costs. The change fit a quirk in its cost offer. Without it, the cost scoring would have lost its power to predict real prices.
gao-gaoreports-b-309752-8:
A plea to rethink a logistics ruling is refused in this GAO decision, B-309752.8, dated December 20, 2007. Kellogg, Brown & Root Services, Inc. sought a fresh look at an October ruling. That ruling upheld protests of Army logistics awards. The deal backs combat troops with global support work. It is known by the short name LOGCAP.

The firm claimed four flaws in the first ruling. It said harm to fair play was not shown. It said GAO used facts outside the score file. It said an audit report was misread. It said talks should not reopen. GAO denied the plea on each point. The first ruling stands as issued.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-8:
Bank rule-making by a federal regulator is examined in GAO-06-8, a report GAO released on October 17, 2005. On January 13, 2004, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued two sets of preemption rules. The rules set how far the National Bank Act overrides state and local laws for national banks. State officials protested both the rules and the way they were written. GAO reviewed the consultation and documentation behind the process.

GAO found that the office generally followed the requirements for rule-making. But it lacked documentation and written guidance for its consultation steps. That gap made its outreach efforts hard to verify. The office did consider all comments on one rule and changed parts in response. GAO saw chances to strengthen both consultation and record keeping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-8:
Reviews of disability benefits are examined in GAO-07-8, dated October 3, 2006. The Social Security Administration must find medical improvement before it can end benefits. That rule guards people on Disability Insurance and Supplemental Security Income. Each year, about 13,800 beneficiaries leave the rolls under this standard. GAO surveyed all 55 state disability determination offices. It asked how often people improve and what makes the standard hard to apply.

Examiners told GAO the rules leave key points unclear. Seven of 11 examiners were unsure when to use exceptions to the standard. Doubt also clouds how much improvement counts as enough. Views on the presumption of continued disability vary as well. Those gaps can make like cases end in unlike ways. GAO urged the agency to clarify its guidance on each point. The agency saw value in more guidance. It doubted the need for more on the exceptions, though.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-8:
Saving for old age now rests mostly on workers themselves. Pay-in plans tied to each worker's own account have replaced most set-benefit pensions over 25 years. GAO-08-8, dated November 29, 2007, measures how much workers hold in such plans and what they may hold at retirement.

Only 36 percent of workers took part in a current plan in 2004 data. The median balance was $22,800, and $60,600 for workers aged 60 to 64. Forecasts for workers born in 1990 show about 37 percent reaching retirement with no plan savings at all. Low-income workers fare worst. The report weighs ideas to widen coverage.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-8:
A doctor discovers poison in his town's baths and gets branded an enemy for telling the truth. An Enemy of the People shares Archer's eighth volume, from 1908, with The Wild Duck, Ibsen's tragicomic study of self-deception. The pairing shows the playwright's two faces in one binding.

Doctor Stockmann rages against the compact majority that prefers profit to honesty. The Wild Duck turns inward, asking whether stripping away comforting lies always heals or sometimes kills. Idealism's fire and the poet's pity stand side by side. Critics rank both plays among the most perfectly built in all drama. English readers meet them in the classic Archer versions.
lecky-england-18th-vol-8:
Georgian England transforms in the eighth and final volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. Steam and factories remake the land and its towns at speed. A religious revival stirs the nation's soul while reformers press the first claims for a wider vote.

Eight volumes end with a country changed beyond all recognition. The old world of farms and coaches gives way to mills and railways. Lecky closes at the threshold of modern Britain with calm survey. His great history stands complete at last. It is vast, fair, and humane: a portrait of a century that made the modern world.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-8:
Part Eight opens with the Professor's Yarn in Chapter 36. The narrator was once a humble young land-surveyor, he says. A California mining-ditch survey sent him on a sea voyage. Three or four weeks aboard ship lay ahead of him.

Three professional gamblers played daily in an upper-deck stateroom. Their door stood ajar, leaking tobacco smoke and profanity. A countrified, good-natured passenger kept seeking his company. Reading and dreaming were the surveyor's passions, conversation was not. Tobacco smoke and profanity escaped through the gamblers' ajar door. The countrified passenger's beaming good nature engaged him despite himself.
nasa-tm-19710010481-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 8 of the Manned Spacecraft Center's Apollo 13 Investigation Team surveyed high-pressure oxygen systems after the April 1970 explosion. This addendum to its final report, dated March 1971, reviews how materials were judged safe for use with liquid or gaseous oxygen. The panel asked whether existing test methods really captured the ways materials catch fire in oxygen.

The introduction explains that qualification had rested on past use or on impact and friction tests, the most common ignition sources. The panel lists other triggers, including sparks, electrical shorts, shocks, and bulk heating, and notes that powered systems break the old assumptions. It also stresses what happens after ignition: whether a material quenches itself, burns slowly, burns fast, or explodes. The report then assesses current liquid and gaseous oxygen test methods and their competence for spacecraft use.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-8:
Volume eight of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, is given to Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms. The volume came out in 1886 under Philip Schaff. Augustine preached and dictated on all 150 psalms across some thirty years of his bishopric.

His method is allegory: every verse of the psalm is heard as the voice of Christ and his church. A psalm's cry of pain becomes the church suffering; its praise, the church rejoicing. The work is vast, uneven, and beloved. Medieval preachers mined it endlessly, and it shaped how the West prayed the psalter. The volume closes the Augustine block of Schaff's first series.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-8:
Basil the Great's letters and select works fill volume eight of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Basil, bishop of Caesarea, organized eastern monastic life and fought for the Nicene faith. His letters alone run to more than three hundred. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

The letters show Basil at work: settling quarrels, begging tax relief for the poor, and coaching young monks. His treatise on the Holy Spirit argues the Spirit's full divinity from the church's worship. His nine homilies on the six days of creation mix scripture with sharp eyes for nature. The volume is the record of a bishop who built hospitals and a theology at once.
peter-s-pence-sailor-s-knots-part-8:
"Peter's Pence" comes from W. W. Jacobs's Sailor's Knots of 1909, and the night-watchman tells it. Sailors, he says, don't bother much about relations, partly because relations expect presents. Peter Russet has just come home after ten months away, money in pocket, with Sam Small and Ginger Dick beside him.

A letter waiting at the office ruins the planned spree. Peter's old uncle George Goodman, unseen for twenty years, is in London for the first time in thirty-three and wants to stay with Peter and be shown about. Jacobs builds the comedy from Peter's dread and his mates' curiosity.
podcast-joerogan-9uhx6ApHD-8:
Filmmaker Andrew Jarecki joins Joe Rogan for episode 2475. Jarecki made The Jinx, the true-crime series that shook its subject. His work often ends with real legal force.

Rogan explores how Jarecki gains trust and then springs truth. They discuss wealth, murder, and the ethics of the craft. Jarecki shares what the cameras caught and missed. The episode grips true-crime fans from the start. Few guests can match a man whose interviews helped put a killer in cuffs, and he tells it all. The craft behind the shock is the real story.
roughing-it-part-8:
Part 8 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter LXXI. The party winds down a hill of old lava to the sea at four in the afternoon. Flow after flow of fire, Twain says, built the island higher over long ages. The rock below is honey-combed with caves, so wells will not hold water and planters rely on rain tanks. In one place lava closed round a grove of cocoa-nut trees, leaving holes that keep the print of bark, knots, branches, leaves, and nuts.

Soon the party sees Kealakekua Bay, where Captain Cook was killed by the islanders nearly a hundred years before. A summer shower falls as the setting sun flames on the bay, and two bright rainbows span it. Two men riding ahead pass through one bow, and for a moment their clothes shine with more than royal splendor.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: The eighth part of Harry Richmond stands here as wrapper only. The book is by George Meredith. The tale itself is not present. Gutenberg's front pages mark it number 57 in the set. They file it as 4451. First posting was January 31, 2002. It stands in edition 10 and ASCII. David Widger made the file.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-8:
Part eight of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter thirty-two, late on a Tuesday, with the village of St. Petersburg still in mourning. The lost children have not been found, and the search has worn out hope.

Public prayers have been offered, and many a private prayer with a whole heart in it, yet no good news comes from the cave. Most searchers have gone back to their daily work, sure the children are lost for good. Mrs. Thatcher lies very ill, calling for her child in her raving, while Aunt Polly's gray hair has gone near white. Then, in the middle of the night, the village bells burst out in a wild peal.
the-changing-numbers-odd-craft-part-8:
W. W. Jacobs placed this short tale in his Odd Craft gathering, under the title The Changing Numbers. The scene is a small living room at eight in the evening, where a tall clock stands in the corner. Mr. Samuel Gunnill comes down the winding stairs with great care and humility.

His daughter Selina seems lost in tending the plants at the window, and no sign of breakfast preparations appears. She snips dead leaves with exact care, waters like a druggist mixing a dose, then sighs with a force no plant could explain. A second sigh draws a meek cough from her father. She turns fast, upright, with surprise and anger mixed in her look, and the talk begins over a white plant at the row's end. Jacobs builds the comedy from such small household signals.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-8:
Volume eight of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with Jesus and the woman taken in adultery. John's text tells how the scribes and Pharisees set her before him as a trap.
